articles.title: Apple May Phase Out Non-Touch High-End MacBook Pros
articles.content: Apple will likely consolidate its high-end MacBook Pro lineup around touchscreen models, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman . Writing in his latest "Power On" newsletter , Gurman questioned whether Apple would keep updating its high-end ‌MacBook Pro‌ models without touchscreens. The company has retained the mini-LED M5 Pro and M5 Max models alongside the new touchscreen versions, which cost $400 more. Gurman cited the resources required to support parallel product lines across development, production, and promotion. Given the price difference, he expects the two offerings to converge, although he did not specify when Apple might stop developing the non-touch models. Gurman added that Apple plans to introduce another generation of touchscreen MacBook Pros in 2027. These machines will use M7 Pro and M7 Max processors with additional hardware capabilities for AI. He previously said the chip upgrade would arrive toward the end of 2027. The redesign will also reach the entry-level 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌, according to Gurman. Apple plans to offer an M7 version with reduced weight, a thinner enclosure, and narrower borders around the display, similar to the new high-end models. Gurman first reported plans for the redesigned base model in July, when he outlined a potential launch in the first half of 2027. Apple unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pros last week, retaining the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips introduced in March. The redesign pairs OLED displays and Dynamic Island with a lighter, slightly thinner enclosure and a revised cooling system that channels warm air away from the screen. articles.title: Apple's Lockdown Mode thwarted by a new persistent iPhone jailbreak
articles.content: A team of hackers has come up with a new jailbreak for the iPhone , demonstrating how it persists with Lockdown Mode on, even after an update to iOS 27.2. Lockdown Mode on iPhone is for users facing grave threats to their digital security Lockdown Mode is Apple's way to harden device security, intended to protect high-profile individuals from sophisticated cyberattacks. While Apple claimed back in March 2026 that it had managed a 100% protection rate since 2022, it seems it's not completely impenetrable. In a video posted to X, hacker group Calif shows an iPhone 18 Pro with Lockdown Mode enabled. A PDF is then sent to the iPhone using AirDrop and viewed. It's still early days for developers and the iPhone Duo, so it's still the case that very many iOS apps look poor on the new device. But those developers who weren't ready on day one, are now starting to support the benefits of the device. Google Maps for iPhone has now been updated to version 26.44.4 expressly to add iPhone Duo support. As always, Google's App Store notes say only that the release features bug fixes, but if you're an existing user, you will see the real benefit immediately. articles.title: AI data centers comprehensively defeated at US midterm elections — 45 measures put on the ballot as Americans overwhelmingly vote against developments
articles.content: Several counties in the U.S. have put data center concerns on the midterm ballot, and early results show that Americans are overwhelmingly voting against them. According to Data Centers on the Ballot , 33 measures restricting data center development have already won, with six more questions leading. Only one measure in Harwood, North Dakota, which adds an extra review process for industrial projects, including data centers, has failed, while a further five have no posted results. This is a major setback for the Trump administration, which has been pushing for AI development in the U.S. , but not a surprising result, as one database has shown that “ America hates data centers ,” with polls showing that 70% of Americans oppose AI data center build-outs . 👨‍💻 THREAD on how data center-related ballot measures are faring tonightdata centers are on the ballot in ~40 localities across 13 states, including proposed bans, votes on specific projects, and recalls of pro-data center politicians November 4, 2026 Note that the issues put to a vote are varied, ranging from outright permanent data center bans to moratoriums, time-limited actions, limitations based on size or consumption, and more. The mid-term elections also resulted in the recall of the mayor and two council members in Piqua, Ohio, and the mayor of Yukon, Oklahoma, for previously supporting data center bans. A second tracker of some 46 data center measures across 10 states reveals that of 33 measures to limit data centers, every single one is set to be passed. Of a further 13 positive measures to permit data centers and their construction, 11 look set to be defeated. Despite the overwhelming opposition to AI data centers, it’s unclear if they will affect projects that are already underway. In fact, out of the 300-plus local data center bans enacted across the U.S., only three developments totaling 2.3 gigawatts have been delayed, with 38 gigawatts expected to come online by 2027, and that investment into the infrastructure is still on track to hit $32 trillion by 2050 . Nevertheless, these votes could affect future developments, especially as the U.S. Senate accuses Big Tech of misleading the public on the advantages of AI data centers. It’s also the reason why OpenAI and Anthropic are scrambling for small data center projects that range in capacity from 20 to 30 megawatts, especially as their hyperscale gigawatt sites face delays. President Donald Trump has taken steps to reduce the impact of data centers on the average citizen, like forcing AI data centers to pay an energy dividend to local communities and making tech companies, state governors, and utility companies promise to pay their own way via the “ratepayer protection pledge.” However, it seems that his effort was too little, too late, to change the minds of voters who are afraid of utility price hikes, noise pollution , and other negative effects that data centers have had on communities where they’ve been built.
articles.author: Jowi Morales

articles.title: Here’s your first look at Google Photos’ upcoming Overnight backups feature
articles.content: Credit: Shimul Sood / Android Authority TL;DR We’re bringing you a preview of Google Photos’ upcoming Overnight backup option. The feature would let you back up media while you sleep or when the phone isn’t in use. It keeps the app running in the foreground and keeps the screen active, but without any manual intervention. Countless people rely on Google Photos to ensure their memories stay handy and accessible, irrespective of which device they use or how often they switch devices. But backing up Google Photos is time-consuming and can often stop midway unless you ensure you keep the app running actively. This can be a hassle if you have hundreds or thousands of photos or videos. Google knows that and is working on an option to keep the phone active so the backup continues without issues. You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.

articles.title: The Download: blended meat, restored sight, and the agentic web
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat. Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef. Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat. Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef . —Meghan McCarron This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones. Find out how the sight-restoring implant works . —Linda Marsa MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts. This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Democrats have dealt tech billionaires a major midterm setback The results could bring tougher scrutiny of AI and data centres. ( CNBC ) + Musk poured millions into Texas, but both his candidates lost. ( Wired $) + Several winners promised to restrict data centre construction. ( FT $) + Stock futures slid as Democrats won big. ( NBC News ) + The tech left said it’s ready to “wipe the floor.” ( Vanity Fair $) 2 Google is shutting off Search for schools that reject AI The company said AI and Search can no longer be untwined. ( CNN ) + Critics accused Google of pressuring schools to adopt AI. ( NBC News ) + AI is the end of search as we know it. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 The Binance hackers used fake job interviews in their record heist They targeted an engineer through LinkedIn. ( NBC News ) + Researchers had repeatedly warned about the tactics. ( TechCrunch ) + The breach could boost demand for specialist crypto custodians. ( CNBC ) 4 Materials maker 3M will pay $7.35 billion to settle “forever chemicals” lawsuits The suits involve PFAS in firefighting foam. ( WSJ $) + New tech could help rid water of PFAS. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Finland is opening a nuclear waste vault built to last 100,000 years It will bury spent fuel 400 metres underground. ( New Scientist $) + It’s time to make new plans for nuclear waste .…

articles.title: Canva reveals major restructuring potentially affecting over a thousand jobs
articles.content: Canva wants to streamline its workforce so fewer employees are working in silos Some workers will be asked to relocate – Sydney hub becomes more important The company continues to improve its AI models and is on track for an increase in revenue Canva has announced plans to relocate, reposition or even cut more than a fifth (22%) of its workforce, equivalent to 1,271 employees, making it "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history," per a company-wide message from co-founder and CEO Mel Perkins. She acknowledged that Canva's organizational structure has become increasingly complicated in recent years due to substantial growth, noting that teams have become divided into "narrow areas of ownership" with too many managers and "more handovers and coordination than necessary." Canva isn't the first company to note this complexity, with plenty of other tech giants also looking to flatten organizational structures and streamline lines of management. Canva confirms major workforce reshuffling and layoffs The change is largely being framed as a company transformation to simplify the workforce structure, rather than purely a cost-cutting exercise. Under the changes, its Product, Growth and Platform teams will be merged into a single Product organization. Canva also wants to reduce the number of specialist and management roles it has, incorporating those responsibilities into broader positions. Third and finally, the company also wants to move closer to home. It seems Sydney will become the main location for more of Canva's product development teams, hence the mention of relocation in Perkins' message. "We know relocating is a big decision for those being asked to consider it, and we're committed to making the process as smooth as possible with comprehensive support," Perkins promised. The CEO also dropped the 'office working' bomb – while many tech giants have already enforced return-to-office mandates, Canva has largely supported hybrid working. From January 2027, hybrid workers will be asked to work from the office two or three days per week, depending on what makes sense for those roles and locations. Workers set to leave the company as a result of the changes will receive at least six months' salary and twelve months of healthcare coverage, among other benefits. Canva isn't asking for company-issued MacBooks back, either. Departing 'Canvanauts' can also apply for $10,000 grants under the Canva Collective Fund to start their own business or community project – "we won't take any ownership or equity in what they create," Perkins confirmed. As for the company itself, it recently confirmed 250 million monthly users and vast model improvements, including a 90% reduction in cost per task with 30x cheaper models that are 5x faster than before. It also had 120 AI researchers developing in-house models as of September, and is on track to deliver a year-over-year growth in revenue this year.

articles.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
articles.content: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows. articles.title: Binance heist began with fake job interviews and a malicious Homebrew download
articles.content: Binance has revealed how North Korean hackers spent months preparing to steal approximately $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency last week. According to a November 3 security report by the exchange, the attackers used a malicious Homebrew installation to compromise one engineer and a fake recruitment process to trick another into installing malware disguised as a coding assistant. "Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign. It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident," the exchange said. Binance says the first known compromise occurred in June, when an engineer in Binance’s Wallet DevOps team searched online for a popular AI coding tool and downloaded an adulterated Homebrew installation. Homebrew is a package manager, used by developers to install and manage various software tools on macOS. Binance says it detected the unusual activity, replaced the engineer’s device, and rotated their associated credentials. However, those moves proved to be too little, too late, as the attackers had already learned about the employee’s role and identified colleagues working on the exchange's wallet infrastructure https://t.co/sU9dUqLQDH November 3, 2026 The incident follows the compromise of another Binance software engineer who was contacted in September through a legitimate job hunting platform by a malicious actor posing as a project director. The fake recruiter arranged two interviews. One involved a purported HR representative who conducted a live video call and shared a social media account containing personal photos and videos to establish credibility, while the second involved someone posing as a CEO of a fictitious company. Near the end of the interview, the engineer was asked to download a coding assignment containing a malicious software repository onto his work computer—a popular social engineering scheme. That malicious code executed during the setup process. At the time, Binance said the malware replaced a legitimate component of the Python version-management tool "pvenv" with a malicious version capable of executing commands and communicating with an attacker-controlled server. The exchange's endpoint security tools did not detect the malware at the time. Those compromises began bearing fruit on October 20, as the attackers used the compromised computers associated with the fake interview and an internal AI tool to gain control over two wallet engineers' devices. They also discovered a container deployment permission token stored on the computer of the engineer initially targeted in June. Later, on October 29, the attackers used stolen credentials to access another engineer's computer, deploy a container, and execute a malicious script. This gave them access to Binance's internal wallet signing service, allowing transactions from five hot wallets outside the exchange's normal withdrawal process. The U.S. FBI directly attributed the theft to North Korea on November 1. ”The FBI is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, on or about October 29, 2026. The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as "TraderTraitor," the agency tweeted . Pyongyang has distanced itself from the hack, describing the U.S. claims as "preposterous nonsense.” Binance said it had since frozen or intercepted approximately $2.85 billion in compromised assets, while 98% of the affected funds have been replenished. The tactics resemble previous North Korean-linked campaigns. WaterPlum attackers previously used fake job postings and coding tests to infect more than 30,000 devices across 100 countries, compromising over 7,000 crypto wallets in September. A 2024 campaign that targeted Python developers with fake job offers and malware hidden in code was attributed to the Lazarus group , which was also linked to the…

articles.title: NASA's Swift Observatory Is Falling to Earth
articles.content: joshuark shares a report from Wired: After 22 years in orbit and a failed rescue mission this summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week. It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft -- which is roughly as big as a large elevator -- will fall. Despite its size, experts say the risk to the public is relatively low. The observatory was designed to operate for a few years in low Earth orbit, but it far exceeded its expected lifespan, helping to make many important discoveries about the evolution of the cosmos, including the study of supernovas and the destruction of stars by black holes. However, in 2024, increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth's atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Without a propulsion system capable of correcting its orbit, its days were numbered. The U.S. Space Force now expects Swift to reenter Earth's atmosphere around November 6. Most of the spacecraft is expected to burn up, although some components could survive and reach the ground (but most likely the ocean). "The most likely survivors are its six heavy reaction wheels, the spinning flywheels it used to aim itself, along with tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors," Dean Sladen, a quality manager and aerospace engineer at Accu Components, told Space.com. "Only a handful of small, scorched fragments are expected to make it down -- nothing recognizable as a telescope." "NASA's own orbital debris requirements state that the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall not exceed one in 10,000, so it is highly likely this work has been completed but not published," Sladen said regarding the risk assessment. "Personally, I believe it should be published, as NASA has done with previous satellites. The risk is almost certainly very small, but it would give people a clear, factual picture rather than guesswork." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: The National STEM Festival is taking its science fair global
articles.content: In 2023, the National STEM Challenge launched with a goal of attracting students to technical fields—including those who wouldn’t have necessarily seen themselves as traditional science types. Roughly three years later, the event—now known as the National STEM Festival —has drawn students from across the country to present innovative projects at its annual gathering in Washington, D.C. The festival, run by the educational media company Explr , has also provided connections with business leaders and public officials for students looking to explore what careers in science might look like for them and how they can take their projects further, whether that means additional research or filing for intellectual property protection. “We’ve been able to connect students with leaders and mentors and just bigger opportunities, so that they could develop their ideas even further,” says Kari Byron, who cofounded Explr and is a former cast member of TV’s MythBusters . Now, the festival is planning to expand abroad, starting with an inaugural United Kingdom festival slated for May 2027. The U.K. event is open to students between 13 and 19 from England, Scotland, Wales, or Northern Ireland, who can apply by November 22 to participate. Up to 40 will be chosen to present their work at the festival in London. As in the United States, part of the goal is helping make STEM fields accessible to people from a variety of communities and backgrounds, so travel and accommodations will be paid, says Jenny Buccos, Explr cofounder and CEO. Students will have the chance to meet a range of potential mentors and supporters . Jenny Buccos (left), Kari Byron (right) [Photo: Courtesy of National STEM Festival] “Very much like the U.S. has federal government participation, one of our events is taking place at the House of Lords,” Buccos says. In the U.S. festival, students have presented projects ranging from a machine to recycle waste plastic into 3D printing filament to to a pill-counting app aimed at pharmacies with limited resources that lack traditional pill-counting machines. In the 2026 festival, which took place in June, about 42% of projects involved artificial intelligence to some degree, according to Explr data, though only about 13.6% were primarily focused on AI and machine learning itself, suggesting students aren’t simply following the latest trends. “The projects are increasingly showing us what young people believe is worth solving,” Buccos says. [Photo: Courtesy of National STEM Festival] In addition to honing and showing off their scientific prowess, students receive help with networking and presenting their ideas, including via a science networking course offered through the festival, Buccos says. There’s even a podcast where some participants have discussed their ideas. “We’re trying to go back and give them the skills that they can carry with them throughout their life, even if they choose to not go into a STEM career,” she says. “Being able to express your ideas and adjust it to an audience is really, really important.” [Photo: Courtesy of National STEM Festival] Students naturally connect with each other through the festival—“They started as strangers, and by the end, these kids are dancing, they’re singing Taylor Swift songs together,” says Byron, the Explr cofounder—and remain digitally connected after they return home. Some have come back to help the next cohort of students present their ideas, and they’ve offered feedback on the festival itself. [Photo: Courtesy of National STEM Festival] The events are unlikely to be limited to the U.S. and U.K. Plans are underway for a festival in Guadalajara, Mexico, in November 2027, and Explr is in early discussions about hosting a regional festival in the United Arab Emirates, focusing on the Middle East and North Africa. “The idea is, we have the Olympics every four years,” says Buccos. “Why aren’t we having innovation summits like this for young people?”
articles.author: Steven Melendez

articles.title: UK policing minister promises new facial recognition laws after criticisms
articles.content: The UK government wants tighter controls over facial recognition tech A public consultation finished earlier this year Privacy groups say the cameras are 'an indiscriminate tool' UK policing minister Sarah Jones has committed to tighter restrictions on the use of live facial recognition (LFR) on the streets of Britain, saying that the technology — which scans and identifies faces in real time from police-operated cameras — will have new "parameters and principles" set by law. As the BBC reports, the announcement comes after a public consultation on how LFR is used across the country. According to Jones, citizens "by and large" support the crime-fighting system, which has been trialled since as far back as 2015, but want more assurances around safety and privacy. "For example, if I had an outstanding parking fine, I would not expect this technology to be used for that," Jones, who is the MP for Croydon West, told the BBC. "We have to use it proportionately. We have to use it in an intelligence-led way. And I think we also have to be clear that there will be some oversight." The Metropolitan Police, which has been expanding its use of LFR in recent years, says the cameras have led to more than 3,000 arrests in the past two years. The tech is typically deployed in a mobile van, but there are plans to increase the number of fixed cameras in parts of the West End and Soho in the capital. Real-time scanning and matching LFR works by scanning faces in real time, and comparing them to a police database of individuals — from missing people to wanted criminals. Every match still needs to be double-checked by a human, and for faces where no match is found, the data is immediately deleted, according to the police. Representatives from privacy group Big Brother Watch have previously described the rollout of LFR tech to static cameras as an "alarming escalation of an intrusive technology" that scans the faces of millions of innocent people without permission. The police are advised to publicly advertise the use of LFR online, unless there's a "critical threat". Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at the Big Brother Watch privacy group, told the BBC that the facial recognition technology was "an indiscriminate tool" that represented something "fundamentally un-British" — going against the presumption that you're innocent until proven guilty. "Thousands of people have expressed their objection to the use of this technology and the government has sat on those responses for over six months," Chaggar said. "All the while, facial recognition has been rolled out in train stations and Tube stations and shops and supermarkets across the country." In the US, similar surveillance systems such as those operated by Flock have come under fire not just for their default capabilities, but also for how they can be misused by police officers and others with access to the cameras — which is something else the UK public will no doubt want assurances about in the future.
articles.author: David Nield
articles.fingerprint: after criticisms facial laws minister policing promises recognition

articles.title: Watchdog sticks probe into Capita's handling of 1.7 million member civil service pension scheme
articles.content: Capita has repeatedly "broken" promises to resolve the "chaos" engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) following its takeover of the administration – a move that left thousands of retired public sector workers unpaid. So says Parliamentary spending watchdog, the Public Accounts Committee, which this week launched an inquiry into the handover of the ten-year £239 million contract in December from previous incumbent MyCSP. As The Register exclusively revealed , the troubles began early on as members of CSPS – which manages pensions for 1.7 million people – complained of unrecognized passwords and usernames on the portal Capita developed. Capita said it inherited 132,100 complex remediation cases, and claimed the work-in-progress backlog from the prior system was more than double the 37,000 items when it won the deal in 2023 . Capita ran to Microsoft for support , and promised the use AI and automation, in addition to its 500 full-time employees working on the project, would resolve the issues by March. It missed this deadline, as well as one set for June 30 and is set to miss March 2027 . The government subsequently withheld a £10 million payment to Capita over the CSPS fiasco. The National Audit Office, a spending regulator, has already launched its own probe into the failures and is now joined by the PAC, which says thousands of civil servants and their families have struggled to on and collect their pensions The PAC has already held three evidence sessions on Capita and the government’s efforts to ameliorate the situation. The law was changed in the Budget 2026 to mitigate the impact of administrative delays in CSPS on bereaved families. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair at the PAC, said in a statement: "In response to the alarming reports of hard-working civil servants being thrown into financial uncertainty following Capita’s takeover of the CSPS, we have held a number of evidence sessions with both the top leadership of Capita, and the civil servants and ministers of the Cabinet Office who have ultimate responsibility for overseeing the contract. " Over and over again, promises have been made and broken by Capita, to our faces in formal evidence sessions, that they will get a grip on what has gone wrong. As a result, we are launching an inquiry, which will be informed by the authoritative factual basis provided by the NAO, which supports the scrutiny work of this Committee." The inquiry will draw on the finding of the NAO's forthcoming report on the switch of CSPS to Capita, and will take into consideration the status of the scheme at go-live date, how Capita has performed, and the effect on CSPS members, plus take a look into the way the Cabinet Office has overseen the prior scheme and the switch to Capita. The Register has asked Capita to comment. ®
articles.author: Paul Kunert

articles.title: Apple's Insider Trading Policy Now Covers Prediction Markets
articles.content: Apple has added an explicit ban on using confidential information to bet on prediction markets to its insider trading policy, according to a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The policy was filed on Tuesday as an exhibit to Apple's annual report on Form 10-K , which is also available on Apple's Investor Relations website . The new version is marked "Updated October 2026," while an earlier version that Apple filed in 2024 doesn't mention prediction markets at all. If you haven't heard of them, prediction markets are basically platforms where people buy and sell contracts that pay out depending on whether a future event happens. The new clause in Apple's policy is titled "No Trading in Prediction Markets Based on Confidential Information," and it warns employees not to "participate in 'prediction markets' or similar platforms to wager, bet, trade, buy or sell contracts based on the outcome of future events," when doing so involves confidential information obtained through their work at Apple. It's not a blanket ban, however. The restriction applies only when confidential information is used, but that also includes information about other companies, such as Apple's suppliers, manufacturers, vendors, customers and carrier partners. Apple also says employees must not share confidential information to others who may go on to use it on such markets. Apple's insider trading policy applies to directors, officers, employees, independent contractors and consultants, as well as to family members who live with them or are financially dependent on them. articles.title: Hackers target French blood banks in latest freezer attack amid UK warnings
articles.content: Hackers have targeted French blood stocks used in medical emergencies Attackers tried to raise freezer temperatures from -22F to 230F The attack was spotted quickly and no blood had to be destroyed A few days ago, hackers attacked European supermarket freezers for the second time in weeks, but it’s not just frozen food that has been the target of these malicious operations. Now, threat actors have their eyes on the medical sector, with reports emerging that French blood plasma reserves have been breached by unknown saboteurs. As reported by Cyberattaque (via Cyber Security News ), stores of blood plasma were struck overnight between November 1 and November 2, with freezer temperatures programmed to rocket from -30C to 110C (-22F to 230F). Although it’s unknown whether the freezers actually reached temperatures as high as that, the incident is still a worrying development in what looks like an ongoing strategy against key infrastructure targets. The campaign targeted Coolworld, which supplies the French Blood Establishment (EFS). The EFS is responsible for collecting, preparing and distributing blood and blood products in France, many of which are used in essential surgeries and medical operations. Cyberattaque noted this meant that “frozen plasma for transfusions was among the potentially endangered products.” The French Ministry of Health has said that the cyberattack did not result in any serious operational consequences because the temperature spikes were noticed quickly and corrected. What’s not known is how many facilities were affected, how long the disruption lasted and how high the temperature of the freezers actually got. However, there has been no confirmation that any blood stocks had to be destroyed as a result. Far-reaching effects (Image credit: Shutterstock) In October 2026, Vincent Strubel, the director general of France’s cybersecurity agency (known as ANSSI), issued a prescient warning that refrigeration facilities — including those storing medical resources — could be the target of adversarial attacks. Two weeks after that address, the blood stores were hacked. Meanwhile, in the UK Richard Horne, CEO of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), yesterday cautioned that “far too many of our organizations and supply chains rest on weak technology and operational foundations.” Potential targets include “Electricity switching, sluice gates in water facilities, dam operations, manufacturing lines, heating, refrigeration controls,” Horne stated. At the launch of the NCSC's 'State of the Cyber Nation' report , Horne went on to describe as the UK as being at a ' Sliding Doors moment' for cybersecurity, with its exploitable vulnerabilities being akin to a "digital Leaning Tower of Pisa". "In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents," he warned. As Cyberattaque pointed out, it was not the medical facilities themselves that were compromised, but the third-party maintenance systems that controlled freezer temperatures. That could have far-reaching effects, as any company that provides controller products to different customers potentially puts them all at risk. While the attempt on the French blood stocks was spotted quickly, the next attack might be able to slip through the net. If that happens, the upshot could be far more serious.
articles.author: Alex Blake
articles.fingerprint: amid attack banks blood freezer french hackers latest target warnings

articles.title: iPhone 18e Rumored to Focus on Chip Upgrade With Few Major Changes
articles.content: Apple's upcoming iPhone 18e will primarily focus on a chip upgrade, with few major new features expected, according to the leaker known as " Fixed Focus Digital ." In a new post on Weibo, the leaker said that a new chip is the only upgrade they can currently confirm for the device. They also claimed that the standard iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e will share some manufacturing processes , while tempering expectations for substantial changes. Fixed Focus Digital drew attention to their correct prediction that the iPhone 17e would retain a notch, despite other sources insisting it would gain the Dynamic Island . The reference could hint that the iPhone 18e will also miss out on the feature, although the leaker did not explicitly say this. The claim follows a recent report from fellow Weibo leaker "Digital Chat Station," who said the iPhone 18e will feature an A20 chip, a 6.12-inch OLED display with a 60Hz refresh rate, and a single 48-megapixel rear camera. That report also suggested a front-facing camera upgrade was possible. The A20 is expected to be similar to the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo 's A20 Pro chip, but feature one fewer GPU core just like its predecessor. The iPhone 18e is expected to launch alongside the standard ‌iPhone 18‌ and the iPhone Air 2 in spring 2027. articles.title: PHP vulnerability post-mortem reveals bug was known two years ago — Small team of maintainers knew of the issue before it was made public, as new PHP2Shell chained exploit ravages servers
articles.content: The phrase "when it rains, it pours" applies both to weather and computer security, as proven the week of October 19, 2026, when OpenAI's GPT 5.6-Sol discovered critical vulnerabilities in the open-source programming language PHP. As published in a post-mortem, a small team of maintainers knew of the issue two years ago. Security experts had warned for decades about mounting technical debt, as agentic AI exponentially sped up vulnerability scanning, to the point that the usual 90-day disclosure window for security exploits became pointless . PHP, one of the internet's ubiquitous software packages, was unlucky enough to in the crosshairs of bug-hunting AI agents. PHP hosts around 70% of websites on the internet, and the vulnerability allows for remote code execution with enough attacker knowledge. That combination is enough to sound alarms, but the situation got worse once the collective internet realized that, at the time, 73% of PHP installations online were running end-of-life versions with no active support — eliciting face-palms from many techies, and an exasperated sigh from anyone familiar with the ecosystem, myself included. So ultimately the problem wasn't really the vulnerability, but the general complacency. How the attack came to be The root cause of the vulnerability was an ancient architectural decision in the PHP engine's error handling. When a PHP process runs out of memory, it'll call the longjmp() C function, which means "immediately jump the execution to another place, no questions asked." Using longjmp() without a very good reason is generally unadvisable, though that by itself wasn't the problem. The real issue is that if that jump happens while building a data structure (like adding an array entry, or initializing an object), that half-baked data remains in the memory heap. When the PHP engine moves execution to its cleanup-end-exit mechanism, that code will execute expecting good, complete data, but instead acts on inconsistent leftover bytes. With some clever injection of just the right content in a web request, this mechanism can be exploited to run any code with PHP's permissions, as shown by the ongoing PHP2Shell exploit. Gaining a remote shell does require an attacker to know the exact version and build of PHP used, so it's not as trivial as just pressing the "Hack" button. Yet the wide blast radius, with tens of millions of vulnerable servers, many of them running the same exact version, is enough to give anyone pause. After the vulnerability was made public, many sysadmins disabled version number reporting on their PHP installation, so as not to aid prospective hackers. The PHP Foundation's post-mortem indicates that the team had known about the issue for two years, but didn't immediately see it as a cause for concern, and went back and forth several times on the best way to fix the problem while maintaining compatibility with third-party extensions. The team admitted it had made management mistakes, but it's a small outfit with one full-time employee and 14 part-time contractors, tasked with maintaining one of the most widespread pieces of software on the internet. This is a common pattern: open-source software that's of critical importance to modern computing , yet undermanned, underfunded, or both. The exploit is only half of the problem The standard patch process is reasonably trivial, needing only a point update and perhaps requiring a restart of some services. The currently maintained branches of PHP are 8.1 through the current 8.5. Sysadmins rarely install PHP directly, though, relying on their Linux distribution of choice or community repositories for updated packages. Those 73% of sites still stuck with PHP 7 are now stuck between a rock and a hard place. When PHP moved from 7.4 to 8.0 in late 2020, there were a number of changes to the language, most of them minor, but still requiring revision work. Many folks likely expected their distro to keep backporting fixes, especially for LTS…

articles.title: I waited years for the iPad mini 8, so why do I feel like Apple is ripping me off?
articles.content: I recently called out Apple’s new “why not” era under CEO John Ternus — a chaotic, experimental chapter bringing us the $2,000 iPhone Duo and $3,000 touchscreen MacBook Pros . Well, the iPad mini 8 just arrived, and it perfectly encapsulates the dark side of this new philosophy. I just finished reading Tony Polanco’s review of the new mini, and I completely agree with his assessment: it is a stunning piece of hardware. That new OLED panel is a visual marvel, the IP67 water resistance is a massive structural win, and it is undeniably one of the most capable tablets Apple has ever made. And then, I looked at the pricing ladder, and realized it revealed something grave. The iPad mini 8 is proof that Apple’s “budget” tier is officially dead, replaced by sneaky paywalls, binned silicon and a display refresh rate that would have been considered “old” back in 2018. By stuffing flagship features into a smaller chassis, compromising weirdly in some areas and passing the skyrocketing component costs directly to you, the message is clear: buying into the Apple ecosystem today comes with a pro tax. The hidden cost of the A20 Pro (Image credit: Apple/Tom's Guide) If the $699 starting price wasn’t concerningly high enough, Apple has incorporated tantalizing silicon upgrades into its price ladder. In all the marketing, the Cupertino crew boasts that the new mini is powered by the 2nm A20 Pro chip from the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max and Duo. But what you don’t see until you actually head to the shop is that if you buy the base model, you aren’t actually getting the full chip. You are getting a slightly nerfed version. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) In fact, if you take a closer look at the specs (5-core CPU, 7-core GPU and 16-core Neural Engine vs the 6-core CPU and dual 16-core Neural Engine), something struck me. This sounds like the difference between the A18 and A18 Pro of last year — knocking a core off. The entry-level and mid-tier models are locked to this binned option. If you want the actual A20 Pro, you’re forced to drop $1,000 on the 512GB version. Now, is this something most people are going to feel? No. But it’s something worth noting. Apple is holding the true A20 Pro performance behind a massive storage paywall. You’re paying MacBook Air to get the real thing. Does RAMageddon fly anymore? (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Many folks at this point will immediately point to the supply chain, and that’s fair enough. We are in the middle of a brutal global memory shortage driven by the AI data center bubble — Ternus himself said it’s “unprecedented” in Apple’s most recent earnings call , and the A20 Pro requires RAM overhead to run Apple Intelligence. But the solution to this component inflation is rather telling. It’s something I’ve talked about with the MacBook PROLED and Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 . I’m gonna call it the OLED facade. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Rather than eating a margin hit to protect entry-level consumers, or finding a way to build a highly capable device with slightly older silicon, Apple’s gone the luxury route — packing an OLED screen into a re-engineered body and jacking up the price. As David Naranjo, Associate Director at Counterpoint Research, told me when we predicted the price of the new MacBook Pros , OLED is “becoming a way for PC makers to justify higher prices as memory and component costs go up.” Companies are “using these premium displays to protect their profits and balance the rising costs." They aren’t just adjusting for inflation; the idea of an accessible budget-friendly tablet is slowly but surely being abandoned. The pro-tier squeeze (Image credit: Tom's Guide) But what I find most frustrating reading Tony’s review is what Apple’s left out here. If you’re going to lure people in with the $699 tablet, and FOMO upsell them to the fully unbinned processor and enough storage, the device needs to be a flawless flagship experience. Yet, despite the price hike, Apple still locked the display to a 60Hz refresh…

articles.title: Google Maps Updated to Fully Support iPhone Duo Displays
articles.content: Google Maps has been updated with improved support for the iPhone Duo's displays, so that the app now fills the foldable iPhone's inner and outer screens rather than leaving unused space along the edge. The change comes with version 26.44.4, which is available on the App Store . Google doesn't mention Duo-specific changes in its release notes, but the updated support is plainly visible. The previous version, 26.43.1, was only partially adapted to the device, and there was still a vertical black border along the right side of both the inner and outer screens, where the circular status bar lives. Now the map extends across the inner screen, with the search field in the upper-left corner, the Explore, You, and Contribute tabs in a panel on the left, and map controls on the right. Google Maps follows a growing number of apps adapting to Apple's foldable iPhone. Earlier this week, Zoom and several Microsoft apps gained Duo optimization, including Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and OneNote. Related Roundup: iPhone Duo Tags: Google , Google Maps Buyer's Guide: iPhone Duo (Buy Now) Related Forum: iPhone This article, " Google Maps Updated to Fully Support iPhone Duo Displays " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: Nvidia can only fulfill 1% of China’s massive $70 billion GPU order for AI chips, report claims — supply constraints choke export-friendly RTX Pro 5500 deliveries despite huge demand
articles.content: Chinese technology giants ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, among others, are set to receive only a limited number of Nvidia chips that they've ordered. Bloomberg is reporting that, according to unnamed sources, only "some tens of thousands, or roughly 1%" of RTX Pro 5500 workstation GPUs will be delivered over the next few months. Go deeper with TH Premium: GPUs (Image credit: Noctua) Desktop GPU Roadmap Nvidia's Enterprise GPU Roadmap Testing DirectStorage with GPU decompression The GeForce RTX 30-series upgrade matrix — does your Ampere GPU need an upgrade in 2026? Rubin in-depth The Stout Owl: The ultimate Noctua G2 PC Demand for the RTX Pro 5500 has far outstripped Nvidia's planned production. According to earlier reports, Chinese firms were suggested to have spent $35 billion on orders for over 3 million of the GPUs , far beyond Nvidia's ability to produce them. This new report suggests that amount has risen to $70 billion, at a cost of $11,000 per unit. Chinese demand for the RTX Pro 5500 is based on its performance and its unique status for shipping. The RTX Pro 5500 has the same CUDA cores as its flagship gaming GPU, the RTX 5090 , but with a boosted 84GB GDDR7 memory count, so it's a good option for AI. Unlike the RTX 5090, or other AI-focused workstation GPUs like the H200 and B300, there are no export limits, meaning it can be shipped to China without restrictions. China is in an arms race with the U.S. to produce better AI models, with GPUs like the RTX Pro 5500 being core to its success. Nvidia has reportedly halted RTX 5090 production to pivot towards its AI-focused enterprise base. The report suggests that Chinese developers expect a first batch of several thousand RTX Pro 5500 GPUs to be delivered by the end of 2026. In total, 700,000 RTX Pro 5500s are expected to be delivered by the end of 2027 as Nvidia increases its production, although this could change. Tom's Hardware has approached Nvidia for comment. In a statement to Bloomberg , an Nvidia spokesman declined to comment on shipment numbers, but did criticize U.S. export controls, stating that "outdated U.S. export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly half a decade ago" continue to restrict it, along with "China's own limits on U.S. imports."
articles.author: Ben Stockton

articles.title: Most Venture Capital Is Going To Companies That Are Founded Or Led By Billionaires
articles.content: The majority of U.S. venture capital nowadays goes to companies founded or led by men who are already billionaires. This is not a difficult stat to unearth. So far this year, just seven companies raised more than half of all seed- through growth-stage investment. They’re mostly familiar names: OpenAI , Anthropic , xAI (now part of SpaceX ), Anduril Industries , Databricks , Prometheus and The Boring Co. These companies raised more than $260 billion in equity funding in the first 10 months of the year. That’s just over 50% of the U.S. seed and venture investment over the same period, per Crunchbase data. Founders and CEOs of these seven companies are also well-known — and exceptionally well-off to boot. The world’s wealthiest men Two founders are particularly famous. They are the world’s wealthiest men: Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos . Musk founded xAI and The Boring Co., and also co-founded OpenAI, (though he has no known equity stake in the latter). And while outside investors funded these companies, Musk could have also afforded to do so himself. Ditto for Bezos, who in 2025 launched the physical AI startup Prometheus, which raised $12 billion earlier this year. Bezos’ own net worth, meanwhile, is calculated at more than $350 billion. AI’s leading names The two highest valuation startups — OpenAI and the soon-to-be-public Anthropic — also have prominent billionaire founders and CEOs. However, they have mixed backstories to their wealth. OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman primarily made his vast wealth through investments in Y Combinator startups, including Stripe and Reddit . Altman has said he does not have an equity stake in OpenAI beyond a sliver from an old YC round. Co-founder Greg Brockman , by contrast, has a larger stake in OpenAI that was reportedly valued around $30 billion earlier this year. At Anthropic, meanwhile, all seven company co-founders have similar-sized equity stakes, and each is worth billions. This includes the AI giant’s most famous co-founder, CEO Dario Amodei . Databricks, Anduril and others Databricks and Anduril, meanwhile, both have founders serving as CEOs who have amassed billion-dollar-plus net worths during their tenures. Databricks co-founder and CEO Ali Ghodsi has a reported $7.6 billion net worth , with the company he leads valued at around $190 billion following an August financing. Anduril co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf , meanwhile, has an estimated $1.5 billion net worth as a result of his stake in the $61 billion valuation defense industry disruptor. Co-founder Palmer Luckey , who sold his virtual reality startup Oculus to Meta for $2 billion in 2014 before starting Anduril, has an estimated $5.9 billion net worth. Several other founders and CEOs of startups that raised some of this year’s largest rounds are billionaires too. This includes Wonder founder Marc Lore , Figure founder Brett Adcock , and Surge AI founder and CEO Edwin Chen , among others. Billionaire categories We can split the billionaires who founded this year’s most heavily funded startups into two broad subcategories. There are those who became billionaires through the startup that just raised capital. And there are those who were already billionaires through prior companies or investments. Ghodsi, Amodei and Brockman fit in the first group. In the second group, of course, we can put Musk and Bezos, as well as Altman and Luckey, who became a 21-year-old billionaire following the Oculus sale. Historically, neither billionaire type was a particularly common recipient of venture funding rounds. The term “unicorn” as a moniker for private companies valued at $1 billion or more only entered the lexicon in 2013, when this asset class became noticeably large. In prior decades, founders and CEOs mostly only hit billionaire status after their startups went public or sold in high-priced acquisitions. Updating the venture archetype But times change. And in tandem, our image of what a startup funding recipient looks like should…

articles.title: Honor is reportedly testing a phone with a record 15,000mAh battery
articles.content: Honor is reportedly testing a phone with a 14,000-15,000mAh battery The main selling point of the handset would apparently be a "guaranteed" week of battery life However, we wouldn't count on being able to buy it even if it does launch After having remained relatively stable for a long time, battery capacities in smartphones have finally started increasing over the last few years, thanks largely to the use of new technologies such as silicon carbon . But mainstream handsets still tend to be under 6,000mAh, and very few phones breach 10,000mAh. That could soon change though, as Honor is reportedly testing a phone battery of between 14,000mAh and 15,000mAh — with the phone’s main feature supposedly being a “guaranteed” one-week battery life. This is according to leaker Digital Chat Station posting on Weibo (via NotebookCheck ), which has a reasonable track record — but we’d still take this with a pinch of salt. The right brand for the job The Honor Win RT 2 (Image credit: Future) If any company was going to do this, Honor would be a likely candidate, as this brand has already launched the likes of the Win RT 2 gaming phone with a 12,070mAh battery. So making a phone with a 2,000-3,000mAh higher capacity doesn’t sound impossible, but it might lead to quite a weighty, chunky handset, or mean compromising other specs. As NotebookCheck points out, it might also require more complicated thermal management, so there are likely to be challenges in delivering this. Still, there could be a market for it, particularly for people who spend a lot of time off-grid or simply use their phones a lot. With the right MagicOS optimization, that one week of life claim could well hold up given that 15,000mAh would be triple the capacity of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra — a phone which delivered “fantastic” battery life according to our review. That week-long battery life would also take Honor's smartphone into the kind of feature phone territory that many of is remember getting from our classic Nokia phones. Although current Nokias, like the Nokia 300 Charge, promise 40 days of standby time and even have a power bank for charging other gadgets. It isn't clear if Honor's phone will come with these kinds of features, and for now we wouldn’t count on seeing it launch globally. Even if Digital Chat Station is right, it only only says that Honor is “testing” it, and even if it launches, it might only be sold in China. Still, if Honor shows that it’s achievable without making the phone ridiculously chunky in the process, it’s possible that other brands will follow suit.

articles.content: Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler. | Bloomberg via Getty Images Search queries are growing at their fastest rate in five years, Google parent Alphabet said in its earnings report last week. Meanwhile, growth in paid clicks - clicks on ads that generate revenue for Google - slowed from 13 percent to 8 percent. articles.title: 'The goal can’t simply be AI usage': New report finds people using AI are working up to 90 minutes extra every day
articles.content: AI users end up working longer days, despite the promise of improved productivity, ActivTrak study finds Heavy AI users could end working up to 90 minutes extra every day Software engineers and operations managers found to be among the highest AI users For years, businesses were told that one of the main advantages of implementing AI in the workplace was that it would lead to greater productivity and efficiency among workers. However new analysis has found that workers who regularly use AI are actually working longer days than those who don't. In fact, the study from ActivTrak discovered that AI users are often working up to 90 minutes longer every day. AI boom or bust? ActivTrak's report looked over digital work activity from over 9,000 employees at 467 companies between April 1 and September 25 2026, and deduced that the workday of an AI userspanned an average of 8.4 to 9.1 hours - compared with 7.6 hours for non-users, a difference of up to 90 minutes each day. 'Heavy' AI users, aka those which used AI tools for more than 45 minutes across at least five sessions a day, also spent an additional 18 minutes working after hours compared with non-users. These users were also found to be switching between applications more frequently, and had shorter periods of "uninterrupted focus" than other workers. There was one silver lining for heavy AI users - the report found they spend much less of their workday in meetings, which took up just 3% of their day, compared to 5% for non-users. Looking at specific job roles, the report found heavy AI users included software engineers, who averaged 0.6 application switches per hour and spent 78.5% of their active time in core coding applications, and operations managers, who were more likely to rely on browser-based AI tools, and spent 75.5% of their active time in core applications and average 1.1 application switches per hour, rising to 4.1 during periods of heavy coordination. “AI may help employees complete tasks faster, but our research shows it contributes to longer workdays, more application switching and shorter focus sessions,” said Gabriela Mauch, chief customer officer and head of the ActivTrak Productivity Lab. “For leaders, the goal can’t simply be AI usage; they need to treat AI usage as a means to measurable gains in productivity, efficiency and business performance.” The report comes days after Gartner found b arely any organizations are seeing real success when it comes to the results of heavily implementing AI in their workplace. It found just 3% of organizations have hit their targets around productivity and efficiency, as well as trying to cut costs across their business using AI, despite three quarters of leaders expecting AI technology to have a significant effect in their organization, with 85% set to spend more on AI in 2027, despite 38% of them already being over budget.

articles.title: Cloudflare engineers optimize DNS build services for twice the speed and 85% lower RAM usage
articles.content: Cloudflare is up to its optimization shenanigans again. Not too long after finding 100 TB of memory savings between the DNS cache's couch cushions , and another 100 TB of saved RAM by improving its task-server routing , the company's engineers are back with the hat trick. This time , they managed to halve DNS zone rebuild times and cut that procedure's memory usage by 85% across its network. A "DNS zone" is the collection of records, settings, and metadata for a given domain like tomshardware.com. The records are the main part, containing IP addresses, hostnames, or text lines including website and mail server IPs, subdomains, domain redirections, and spam-control or certificate info. If you're a Cloudflare customer, when you update a record pointing your website to a new IP, or change one of the domain's settings, the service pushes this information onto its many thousands of DNS servers. This sounds easy enough until you realize that Cloudflare's DNS fleet is huge, and that the company now gets 800 zone changes per second, up from 250 four years ago. All those changes add up to enormous amounts of RAM and network traffic. Consistency across the entire fleet must be guaranteed, too, as you can't have one DNS server saying your website is at one place, while another server says it's elsewhere — except during actual transitions, of course. Furthermore, some domains hosted at Cloudflare have over 20 million records, making them exceedingly difficult to build in memory. (Image credit: Cloudflare ) The easy solution, then, is to only update the data that's needed, and that's precisely what the company did for domain records back in 2022 . Updating records is simple: you just write the new value in and propagate it. Altering settings, though, is way trickier. For example, toggling Universal SSL for a domain can trigger a cascade of record updates. Some metadata keys are shared across multiple zones, necessitating an update across all of them. Change events can come in from many Cloudflare services, too, and often didn't have a reason attached, so it was hard to know if other subsequent changes were necessary. Consequentially, setting updates required a full build for safety. The engineers then carefully laid out a plan to optimize this process. First, they tweaked their internal software so that zone change events include a reason and additional information, so that said event can be properly classified. With that info in hand, specific setting changes can use smaller and shorter builds among given types. For example, apex and metadata changes (like UniversalSSL) comprise one. Likewise, changing a domain's nameserver or wildcards also triggers a smaller procedure. Full builds are only used in cases where there is no partial build mechanism. Finally, domains with a large number of records are now updated piecemeal. Cloudflare saw a 85% drop in RAM usage for Zone Builder servers, from 50-79 GB to down to close to 7 GB, mostly due to these changes alone. (Image credit: Cloudflare) The second optimization pass was combining two formerly separate planning and implementation schedulers into just the one, and improving how it operates. The new scheduler detects if several changes apply to the same zone and combines them. Cloudflare uses Apache Kafka for event messaging, and the team changed how the scheduler acts when a message triggers a slow build. Since Kafka only lets messages advance in sequence, the scheduler waited for that job to finish and didn't process requests that arrived in the meantime. Now, it'll acknowledge and run incoming smaller jobs arriving in the meantime. Before, there was always a steady long queue of requests waiting to be processed, as requests piled up and were completed in bursts. Now, they're fulfilled very shortly after being issued, and in a consistent cadence. This significantly improved concurrency capacity, so the team chose to tighten the queue processing intervals. articles.title: I asked a cybersecurity expert how to shop more safely with AI — these are their 5 non-negotiables
articles.content: We’ve gotten to the point where people are relying on AI assistants to help them navigate all the madness associated with holiday shopping. According to Bain & Company , nearly a quarter of US online shoppers plan to kick off their holiday shopping on an AI platform like ChatGPT or Gemini (which is a stat that’s up from 17% last year). With that increase in AI tools being used to aid online shoppers comes the threat of scammers, who look to exploit those shoppers with fake online stores (which are now popping up at a current rate of one every three minutes ). And what’s worse is that those same stores have now started showing up in AI assistants’ product recommendations. In a bid to learn more about how to shop more safely when using AI for online shopping, how a holiday gift list given to AI could build out an identity map of your family and more, I spoke to cybersecurity expert Serena Sullivan . Here’s hoping her advice makes your AI-assisted holiday shopping experience less susceptible to any sorts of scams. (Image credit: Shutterstock) When someone asks an AI assistant to help with their holiday shopping, what personal information might they be revealing about themselves without realizing it? Consumers often unintentionally disclose personal information. Depending on the way the user crafts their prompts into the AI engine, some information could be inferred. For example, if the user is searching for personal care items to purchase as a gift, they could unintentionally reveal the gender and age of the person they are purchasing the gift for. If they search for ballet shoes, they could reveal the age range of the recipient, the gender, their hobbies and interests. If you are looking for gifts that are very expensive versus inexpensive, some conclusions could be drawn about the user’s disposable income. If the person was looking for an experience instead of a gift, maybe a family trip to a theme park, AI could likely deduce the size of the family, whether any family members need accessibility options, which state or country they live in, and a generalization of how much income the family has access to. Individually, these details might seem harmless. However, when combined, they can create a surprisingly detailed picture of someone's personal life. This is how a data aggregation attack works. An attacker can pull information using Open Source Intelligence (OSINT), meaning information that is freely available on the internet, to compile a detailed profile of the individual. This information can then be used to perform detailed phishing or other social engineering attacks through email, voicemail, phone, or text. Treat AI assistants as you would any other online service. Only share the information you are willing to disclose, keeping in mind that other information could be combined to create a detailed picture of the user and those they are purchasing gifts for. Treat AI assistants as you would any other online service. Only share the information you are willing to disclose, keeping in mind that other information could be combined to create a detailed picture of the user and those they are purchasing gifts for. If an AI shopping assistant recommends a website that looks real, how can shoppers tell whether it’s actually a scam or not? And what new warning signs should they keep an eye out for? Just because AI makes a recommendation does not mean that AI found the correct website and does not indicate that the website has been vetted for safety or security. Additionally, AI could present the shopper with an outdated link. When you click a link provided in AI results, the first thing to check is if it is a secure website. For example, if the shopper is warned that the digital certificate is out of date or illegitimate, do not continue using that website. articles.title: Open source project renders your Windows 11 desktop using the NPU rather than the GPU — ‘npu-driver’ can only run at 2 to 3 Hz, targets 30 Hz performance
articles.content: A developer group by the name of labscommunity has released a prototype driver for Windows 11 that renders the desktop using an NPU instead of the system’s (i)GPU. The new driver is called npu-driver, and the open-source (Apache 2.0) code is available on GitHub. It has been tested on Intel Panther Lake systems, and while it isn’t hitting its 30 Hz performance target yet, it is clever enough to fall back to GPU on request or on any fault. (Image credit: labscommunity on GitHub ) The reasoning behind the development of this driver may strike a chord with those observing the 2020s processor landscape. “Every new laptop ships an NPU that sits idle while the GPU composes the desktop, runs the browser and, increasingly, runs local models,” notes the npu-driver readme file. “The question this project asks is narrow and testable: can the NPU take over desktop composition, end-to-end, without the applications or the compositor knowing?” My NPU's activity graph, today (Image credit: Future) Thankfully, the answer to the question about whether the NPU can render the Windows 11 desktop - and apps like Notepad and Edge windows - is a yes. The npu-driver functions as intended and as demonstrated. Moreover, it seamlessly switches back to GPU rendering if/when it needs to. The developer admits that this driver is strictly “a research prototype, not a product” at this stage, and the main issue currently is performance. The GitHub readme notes that the target 30 Hz performance isn’t very close right now, with actual screen refresh speeds of around 2 to 3 Hz. npu-driver is being developed on a Panther Lake laptop , and all these Intel processors feature NPU 5 architecture silicon with performance spanning 45-50 TOPS. Render your entire Windows desktop on the NPU instead of GPU from r/LocalLLM A Reddit post that appears to be penned by one of the labscommunity crew says that this project might render Windows 11 visuals rather slowly, but it can “bring 3D GPU usage down from 3.4% to 0.6%,” thus freeing up the GPU for other tasks, like inference . Having a(nother) useful task for the system NPU to do is a welcome development, even if it seems of rather niche appeal for now. There are no signs consumer processors will abandon NPU integration, and these accelerators will likely remain alongside other now-essentials like hardware for video (de)coding, DSPs, and so on, even if the Copilot+ PC branding exercise has been abandoned by Microsoft and its partners.

articles.title: Cleaning up your Google Photos library might soon take just one prompt
articles.content: TL;DR Google Photos v8.0 contains code that could let Ask Photos delete, archive, share, save, and add photos to albums in bulk, with a cap on how many photos you can select at once. Before deleting, Ask Photos could show how many items it will remove and how much storage you’d free up, let you review its picks, and send everything to Trash so you can recover it later if needed. Ask Photos could also edit multiple photos from a single request. Google hasn’t announced these changes yet. Cleaning up a Google Photos library is one of those chores that everyone puts off. Google Photos does let you select a bunch of photos and delete or archive them, but finding the right ones across years of screenshots, duplicates, and blurry shots is the hard part, and the mess only grows with time. Ask Photos can already find specific photos for you using natural language, but it stops there. That could soon change, as Google appears to be working on letting Ask Photos act on what it finds, in bulk. You’re reading an Authority Insights story. articles.title: Cyberattack on French plasma stores is enough to make your blood boil
articles.content: Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said. The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products. The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion. "The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said. "Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities." The EFS did not name the supplier publicly. According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature. The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health. News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes. Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food. The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday. Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed. Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain. No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting. The latest wave of cold-store attacks comes a month after the first, which affected French supermarket chains Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others. Both supermarket waves involved remote interference with refrigeration controls, causing stock losses. Whether the attack affecting EFS used the same access route remains unclear. Some affected chains identified Danfoss controllers in their systems; others said they did not use the company's equipment. CERT-FR published an advisory at the time of the attacks urging organizations to remediate vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers. The attacks in France followed reports of compromises at US military commissaries, which also led to food wastage in August. ®
articles.author: Connor Jones

articles.title: Upgrade to an OLED display for only $269 at Walmart — Acer's 27-inch Nitro gaming monitor has a superfast 240Hz refresh rate and crisp WQHD resolution
articles.content: You can pick up this 27-inch Acer Nitro (VG277U Xbiip) from Walmart for the staggeringly low price of just $269 . A QD-OLED gaming monitor for this price is an absolute steal. The rise of OLED panel technology for gaming monitors has been one of the best things for PC gamers seeking extra fidelity, color, and contrast. OLED panels offer rich color and blacker blacks along with insanely fast gray-to-gray response times. This type of monitor came with a premium price tag originally, but as the technology has matured, the prices have come down a great deal. ● Grab this deal at Walmart The Acer Nitro VG277U sports a fast 240Hz QD-OLED panel with a 27-inch screen. The display is rated at 400 Nits of brightness, which is more than adequate for a bright display, even in well-lit rooms. The gray-to-gray response time is only 0.03ms due to the OLED tech, which makes gameplay feel incredibly smooth and eliminates ghosting in games with rapid movement. A crisp 2560 x 1440 pixel (WQHD) resolution means sharp images and clear pictures with 99% DCI-P3 color gamut. For help eliminating any screen tearing from a mismatch between game framerates and screen refresh rates, the Acer Nitro VG277U comes with AMD FreeSync Premium. If you're currently using an IPS or VA-based monitor, a QD-OLED display is a massive step up in response times and color accuracy, and can increase your immersion in your favorite games. Nitro VG277U Xbiip: was $349.99 now $269 This mid-sized 27-inch gaming monitor sports a QD-OLED panel rated at a decent 400 nits of brightness, with a 240Hz refresh rate and a resolution of 2560 x 1440. If you're after a gaming screen on a budget and want inky blacks and saturated colors, this is a tough deal to beat. View Deal The Acer Nitro VG277U comes with a good amount of connectivity that includes plenty of video ports. You can expect to find 2x HDMI 2.1 ports and 1x DisplayPort 1.4 port. If you want to connect the screen directly to an audio source like headphones or external speakers, there's a 3.5mm headphone output port.

articles.title: Samsung’s mysterious Galaxy T1 fitness earbuds are getting ready for a US launch
articles.content: TL;DR Samsung’s unannounced Galaxy T1 sports earbuds have received FCC certification in the US. The filings reveal prototype hardware details, Bluetooth testing results, and a charging case diagram. Previous leaks suggest an ear-hook design, customizable controls, and a 595mAh charging case, although launch details remain unknown. Samsung’s next workout earbuds are getting quite the regulatory workout themselves. After making stops in China, South Korea, and Indonesia, the mysterious ear-hook earbuds have now crossed another important finish line: US certification. And unlike previous sightings, this one gives us a closer look at what Samsung has been cooking. The unannounced earbuds, identified by model number SM-R545 and codenamed Galaxy T1, received FCC approval on November 4, 2026. The filings cover both earbuds individually, under IDs ZCASMR545L and ZCASMR545R, marking their first known appearance in the US certification database.
