articles.title: The Saucony Endorphin Speed 5 is just $129 thanks to this early Black Friday deal — at that price, it’s better value than the new Endorphin Speed 6
articles.content: The Saucony Endorphin Speed has been one of the best running shoes on the market ever since the original launched in 2020. It’s always been one of the most versatile shoes available thanks to its fast, comfortable ride, and I loved the Saucony Endorphin Speed 5 when I racked up over 60 miles in it for my four-star review. The new Endorphin Speed 6 just launched, and that’s resulted in some great deals cropping up on the Endorphin Speed 5, which is $129 in the Amazon sale right now. The Endorphin Speed 5 is a super-trainer with a nylon plate and a comfortable but quick ride that makes it ideal for all kinds of daily training runs. Most colors and sizes of the shoe are reduced on Amazon right now, making it a better value buy than the new Endorphin Speed 6 in my opinion. View Deal For me that discount makes it the better buy ahead of the new shoe, because although Saucony has made some changes to the Endorphin Speed 6, the overall ride feel is still similar based on my early testing. What are the key changes to the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6? (Image credit: Future) The main change made to the Endorphin Speed 6 is that it uses a new midsole foam called PWRRUN PBX, which is meant to be a little lighter and softer than the PWRRUN PB foam on the Endorphin Speed 5. Saucony also slightly increased the midsole stack height in the new shoe by 2mm, so it is a little more cushioned all round than the Endorphin Speed 5, while also making minor updates to the upper and outsole, and adjusting the shape of the nylon plate in the midsole. Saucony Endorphin Speed 5 vs Endorphin Speed 6 (Image credit: Future) On paper the updates sound significant with the new shoe, but when I did my first run in the Endorphin Speed 6 it certainly felt very familiar. The midsole foam is a little softer, but still quite firm, and the Speedroll rocker on the shoe pushes you smoothly onto your forefoot at both easy and faster paces. I very much enjoyed the run in the Speed 6, but I was surprised how similar to the Speed 5 it felt, so I actually ran in both shoes at the same time to compare them directly. (Image credit: Future) There are slight differences – the new shoe is marginally softer at the heel in particular — but overall I do think they have a similar ride feel. While the Speed 6 might be a slight upgrade overall, I’d certainly be happy grabbing the older shoe in the sale for $50 less, since the Endorphin Speed 6 will set you back $180 right now.
articles.author: Nick Harris-Fry

articles.content: Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0. Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3. articles.title: Samsung Galaxy S27 leaks reveal bold new Ultra design — and disappointing 'Pro' downgrade
articles.content: The Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra is coming in early 2027, and while we haven't heard a lot about the phone so far, it looks like the floodgates are starting to open. The latest leaks seem to reveal more details about the phone's design, as well as a possible performance change that could prove very disappointing for those of you hoping to pick up the new S27 Ultra. We've already seen design leaks that showcase the Galaxy S27 Ultra's new look , swapping the vertical camera array for a horizontal camera bar — which is reminiscent of the "Raised Plateau" Apple debuted on iPhone 17 Pro Max . Now dummy units of that design have appeared online courtesy of Android Headline , letting us visualize that design as a real phone. Dummy units are, of course, no substitute for the real thing. However they do give us an idea of what using these phones might be like. (Image credit: Android Headline) Takeaways from the dummy units include changes to the camera, which includes removing the 10MP telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom. The telephoto does look quite small, but that's only because the S26 Ultra's telephoto had a deceptive design. So it's unclear what this means for the camera hardware. The actual dimensions of the phone haven't really changed. The S27 Ultra dummy unit measures 163.76 x 78.25 x 7.97mm (6.44 x 3.0 x 0.31 inches), compared to 163.6 x 78.1 x 7.9mm on the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Which means the size difference is barely distinguishable. So really, the main visual changes come in the form of the camera setup. Android Headline also notes that the design includes a built-in S Pen, alongside magnets to facilitate full Qi2 wireless charging. I don't see the magnets on the dummy unit or the CAD renders they're based on, so take that particular rumor with a healthy dose of scepticism. A strange performance split (Image credit: Android Headline) Those of you hoping for a super-powered S27 series may be disappointed, though. While we fully expect that the Ultra model will come with the newly-unveiled Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 (or a custom "for Galaxy" variant), the same may not be true of the S27 Pro. Notebookcheck recently uncovered listings for all four Galaxy S27 models in the import-export database NBD. It reveals that the S27 Pro may come with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 , the successor to the current Elite Gen 5 chipset in the S26 series. This chip is still being build on a 2nm process, with all the performance and efficiency benefits that affords, but it's not the absolute best chip Qualcomm will have on offer. The Extreme Gen 6 chip is supposed to come with better computing, graphics and neural performance, as well as the ability to record videos in 8K resolution at 60 frames per second. (Image credit: Android Headline) The regular Elite Gen 6 is limited to 30fps, and while the ability to record in 8K isn't going to appeal to everyone, it shows that the Extreme chip is the superior option. Certainly from a performance point of view, and that could be enough to push people away from the Pro model. That said, a less impressive chip is likely cheaper, and means Samsung could be trying to avoid unnecessary costs that would need to be passed on to the consumer. The listings also reveal that the international versions of the S27 and S27 Plus could run on the Exynos 2700 chipset, rather than a Snapdragon chip. Though Samsung has been doing that for years, and it's not really that surprising. The same listings feature screen size too, with the S27, S27 Plus and S27 Ultra offering the same 6.3-, 6.7- and 6.9-inch displays as their predecessors. Meanwhile the Pro is set to offer a 6.5-inch display, and sit between the S27 and its plus-sized counterpart. The Galaxy S27 series is expected to arrive in January, and we here at Tom's Guide will be watching for all the latest news and rumors to keep you up to date. Stay tuned for more. articles.title: Dreaming of a white Christmas? The Old Farmer’s Almanac forecast is in
articles.content: Since I flipped my calendar over to November, I feel I can officially start thinking about Christmas. The weather forecasters at The Old Farmer’s Almanac are thinking about it too. But while I’m gathering the ingredients to make homemade mincemeat, they’ve been checking the skies for snow and whether we’ll have a white Christmas this year. What counts as a white Christmas? (Image credit: Getty Images) According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) a white Christmas can be declared when their is at least one inch of snow on the ground on Christmas Day. It doesn’t have to snow on December 25th, as long as a decent covering remains. Will there be a white Christmas where you live? (Image credit: The Old Farmer's Almanac) Their newly released winter outlook divides the continent into starkly contrasting camps, with the chance of a white Christmas varying by region. A white Christmas There are only three regions where the Old Farmer’s Almanac predicts a white Christmas for sure. If you live in the Northeast, the High Plains and Alaska, you can expect a decent covering of snow on Christmas Day. Chance of a white Christmas Although only three regions have a guaranteed white Christmas, a few others have a good chance of a flurry, including the Lower Lakes, Ohio Valley, the High Plains, and the Pacific Northwest. And the Appalachians are divided; if you live in the north, you’re unlucky to see snow, but there is a chance for those in the south. Better luck next year If you were hoping for a white Christmas, you will be disappointed if you live in the Atlantic Corridor, the Southeast, Florida, the Deep South, and the Upper Midwest. If you live in the Heartland, Texas-Oklahoma, the Desert Southwest, the Pacific Southwest and Hawaii, you will also go without. articles.title: My first Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 phone doesn’t live up to the hype
articles.content: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority When we first went hands-on with Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor back in September, its headline features had me excited. With CPU clock speeds reaching 5GHz, a massive 16MB Oryon Flex Cache, and Qualcomm’s next-generation Adreno GPU, the chip promised a major leap in performance for demanding workloads such as emulation and gaming. Benchmarking Qualcomm’s Gen 6 Reference Phone backed up these promises. I’ve since spent the past week with the REDMAGIC 12 Pro , my first retail phone powered by Qualcomm’s new silicon. With 16GB of LPDDR5 RAM and a substantial active cooling system, it should deliver a compelling showcase of next-generation performance that you can actually buy.

articles.title: Disgruntled software developers start ambitious open-source revolt, using AI to clone common services — OccupySaaS AI-powered project wants to kick Auth0, Salesforce, and other pricy service-as-software to the curb
articles.content: AI-powered software cloning is quite the hot topic. Software companies are likely unhappy with the notion of vibe coders ganging up to try and copy their software. Simultaneously, users tired of subscription models, price hikes, and drops in software quality are more than happy to rebel, as proven by the buzz around the Adobe-replacement ArtCraft . Now, OccupySaaS is the latest user-led revolt against the software system, aiming to create clean-room, open-source reimplementations of common services using AI tools. The initiatives already underway in the project look to replace Auth0 and Salesforce with minty fresh alternatives called ZeroAuthy and SalesCompel , respectively. Given that these services all run on their companies' servers, there are no binaries to examine and decompile — the reimplementations are done referencing available documentation, APIs, development kit behaviors, and any applicable open standards. Judging from the project website, it seemingly wants new software to acts as a API-compatible drop-in replacement where applicable. The project puts a sharp pin on its development ethics and requirements: all work must be a fully clean-room reimplementation, with no decompiled code, no confidential information (including source code) taken from any previous employers, and no copying of UI assets or any other trademarks. Creating software in this manner is both easier and harder than usual. On the one hand, the only thing that matters is that whichever user inputs are processed and produce the same outputs as the original software, and those behaviors are largely defined by the aforementioned specifications. At the same time, hosted software is effectively a black box with internal behaviors and "gotchas" that aren't immediately obvious. Just as with console emulators, any drop-in replacement needs to reproduce extant API bugs to be fully compatible — looking at you, Jira. Besides the aforementioned services, OccupySaaS intends to find replacements for services offering document-and-wiki management, issue tracking, software feature flagging, software/server observability, and customer support. Our guesses for the targeted replacements in each of those categories are Confluence, Jira, LaunchDarkly, Datadog, and Zendesk. The language of choice is Go, picked over Rust simply because it allows for easily compiling and linking all its dependencies into the one binary that doesn't need an installer and can just be copied to a target system and executed. According to OccupySaaS, that characteristic makes it ideal for packaging into a Docker container or other forms of self-hosting. Some people may quickly point out that the entire point of renting a SaaS to begin with is that any snafu with the code or the infrastructure is always Someone Else's Problem, and that running your own instance is backwards. However, since OccupySaaS's software is Apache 2.0-licensed , there's nothing stopping anyone from providing a service for it. Examples include Red Hat Enterprise Linux, GitLab, and of course, Wordpress. The project appears to be the brainchild of Thomas Meadows, a software engineer with two decades of experience. In his personal homepage , he claims is strong suit is project management, which is a good skill to have in this day and age of directing AI agents towards a goal. The website reads like a manifesto, pointing out that per-seat licensing taxes growth, and that the same people who created the software are now being fired — "the software built by the 99% belongs to the 99%."

articles.title: Google Photos could soon show some more love to your RAW photos
articles.content: TL;DR Google is working on a new “RAW images” section in Google Photos’ Collections tab. This section will display all the RAW images backed up in Google Photos. The feature isn’t live right now, but we managed to surface it with some tinkering. Most Android phones these days can shoot RAW photos right out of the box. While that is great for image quality and offers better control while editing, RAW files also take up a lot of space. This can quickly turn into a problem when they begin eating into your Google account storage. It can also be difficult to find RAW photos in the app when you want to edit them. Fortunately, Google seems to be working to fix both those problems. You’re reading an Authority Insights story. articles.title: Tech layoffs: A 2026 timeline
articles.content: Among a range of factors leading to a wave of tech sector layoffs in 2026 is the rapid rise of artificial intelligence and automation. Companies are reconfiguring their workforces to leverage AI for increased efficiency and reduced operating costs. This realignment and reduction is implemented even by companies reporting strong financial performance. But it’s not just AI leading to workforce cuts. Complementing this technological shift are ongoing economic uncertainty, inflation, and higher interest rates, compounded by a chip shortage and rising energy costs. This mix is driving companies to cut costs and streamline operations for increased efficiency. According to data compiled by Layoffs.fyi , an online tracker that keep tabs on job losses in the technology sector, 139,004 tech employees have been laid off at 345 companies so far in 2026, compared to the 122,606 layoffs it reported in 2025. Here is a list — to be updated regularly — of some of the most prominent technology layoffs the industry has experienced recently. Notable tech layoffs in 2026 Canva Oracle (again) Monday.com Microsoft Meta Cisco Cloudflare Oracle Atlassian Salesforce Amazon Ericsson Nov. 3, 2026: Canva lays off 22% of staff as it flattens org chart and consolidates teams Canva didn’t explicitly blame AI for a massive round of lay-offs that will see 1,271 staff, over one-fifth of its workforce, lose their jobs, but CEO Melanie Perkins did give a nod to how “ New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use ” in an open letter outlining the changes. To simplify and speed up decision-making around product development, she wrote, Canva is folding its product, growth, and platform teams into a single product organization, removing layers of middle management, reducing specialization by giving staff broader responsibilities, and requiring staff to show up more often at its office in Sydney, which will become the hub for product development. Sept. 15, 2026: Oracle forecasts 33% increase in restructuring costs as new round of layoffs hits Oracle began a new round of layoffs this week, sending early-morning termination emails to staff for the second time in six months. Oracle has made no public statement confirming the latest round of job cuts, but in a regulatory filing days earlier the company said it had set aside a further $700 million for restructuring charges, bringing the total charges this year to roughly $2.8 billion. July 22, 2026: Monday.com cuts 20% of its workforce to restructure for the AI era The company says the decision to cut 620 jobs isn’t about margins, but about creating a flatter organization built around AI agents, autonomous teams, and deeper customer engagement. July 6, 2026: Microsoft cuts 4,800 jobs, primarily in sales and Xbox teams As the company trims thousands of jobs , it’s also investing in embedded engineering teams and AI infrastructure. The layoffs come several weeks after the company offered 8,750 US employees voluntary retirement buyouts . June 5, 2026: Tech industry cut 38,242 jobs in May, worst since 2024 AI was blamed for 40% of the job cuts in May , up from 7% in January, according to research by employment placement company Challenger, Gray & Christmas. May 20, 2026: Meta cuts 8,000 jobs, around 10% of workforce The cuts are expected to expected to hit Meta’s engineering and product teams the hardest, arriving as Meta pivots toward AI to boost efficiency across its organization, according to Yahoo Tech . May 13, 2026: Cisco to cut nearly 4,000 jobs despite strong growth in AI, enterprise networking Despite reporting positive financial news — including record third-quarter revenue of $15.8 billion, a 12% year-over-year increase — Cisco said it will eliminate almost 4,000 jobs . May 7, 2026: Cloudflare to cut 1,100 jobs in AI-focused restructuring About 20% of Cloudflare’s global workforce will be culled as the company pivots for the agentic AI…

articles.title: Google Photos could finally learn to do your photo chores
articles.content: TL;DR Google Photos v8.0 contains code for an upgraded Ask Photos feature that can carry out tasks. We got it to find, enhance, and add photos to a new album from a single request. Ask Photos showed each step as it works, checked before saving anything, and then suggested follow-ups like sharing the album or making a collage. Google Photos’ Ask Photos could also get a new collapsible overlay, and shortcuts to Photos tools and sections. Google hasn’t announced these changes yet. Google Photos packs a couple of AI features, but one of its primary ones, Ask Photos, largely functions as a glorified conversational search bar. Ask Photos lets you use natural language to ask complex questions about your library. You’d think it would help you organize your messy library , but it stops short after locating specific photos and videos, and that’s about it. That could soon change, as Ask Photos appears to be getting one of its biggest upgrades yet, one that could turn it into a full-fledged task engine, complete with a new overlay interface similar to Gemini’s. You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time never gets old
articles.content: Breath of the Wild changed everything. Two decades after The Legend of Zelda made the transformational shift to 3D, Breath of the Wild reinvigorated the franchise with an open-ended adventure that was built around player freedom and expression. Instead of following a set path, players could go wherever they wanted and tackle challenges in a variety of ways. That philosophy filtered down to subsequent games, letting players author their own creative solutions to puzzles in titles like Tears of the Kingdom and Echoes of Wisdom . As a result, Zelda has never been bigger , and the traditional, more linear Zelda games had become a thing of the past … Read the full story at The Verge.

articles.title: Achieving nirvana: Enlightenment 0.28 hits the desktop
articles.content: Fresh on the desktop this week is a new version of Enlightenment as well the continuation of noughties hero KDE 3, the Trinity Desktop Environment, for those who prefer things a little old school. Enlightenment version 0.28 is the latest release of one of the older Linux graphical environments, which first appeared in 1997. Version 0.28 arrives nearly two years after the previous release – we reported on Enlightement 0.27 in January 2025. If you're not familiar with this venerable window manager, often referred to as just E, we refer you back to that article, which also explains Enlightenment's slightly strange version numbering scheme. Last time around we noted that its single-line release notes really didn't give us much to write about. The development team has made up for it this time, with some 68 lines of changes. It's both the same old E, and simultaneously a modern tool: it is still an X11 window manager, but it can also act as a Wayland compositor if you prefer. It offers conventional stacking resizable windows, but also can act as a tiling window manager if you prefer. On recent distros, it can now talk to the Pipewire audio server, and it can also work with NetworkManager to control network connections. This version delivers preliminary support for NetBSD too. This isn't really a tool for newbies or those looking for a simple easy desktop. A sign of its age is that the first-run wizard asks if you want windows to activate as soon as you move the mouse pointer over them. This was traditional 20th century Unix behavior, and in the early days of Linux it was called "focus-follows-mouse," but it's rarely seen today. E isn't a full desktop environment: it only offers a few of its own optional tools, such as the Ecrire text editor, Ephoto picture viewer, Evisum task manager, and Rage video player. Even its taskbar is optional. It is more like a basis for experienced users to customize and build their own environment around. Trinity is back The Trinity Desktop Environment has a rather lower learning curve: TDE is a port of the final version of KDE 3 to modern Linux. Proving old school is still cool, the project – which keeps the look and feel of 2005-era KDE 3.5 alive – has just announced TDE release 14.1.7 , with dozens of bug fixes and plenty of new features. Among these is a tweak to the kicker/taskbar: you can now scroll the taskbar using the mouse wheel, flicking through your open applications.This release drops support for Ubuntu 24.10 "Oracular Oriole" but adds support for the latest 26.10 "Stonking Stingray." Forks of older versions by users disenchanted with new versions are a recurring feature of the FOSS world, but they often tend to peter out after a while. TDE is one of the exceptions: we first reported on a new release in 2021 and again in 2023 . ®

articles.title: Get a load of Excel’s new multi-value cells
articles.content: Until now, Microsoft Excel has followed a strict structural rule: each cell on a worksheet can hold only a single scalar value. While you can string together text using commas or write dynamic array formulas to spill values across adjacent rows and columns, the cell itself remains a single-item container. But Excel has evolved. A feature currently in preview lets you store multiple distinct, structured values within a single cell. Three new data structures can now be put inside a cell: A list maintains a sequence of independent values arranged in a single column. Unlike a plain text string separated by commas, an in-cell list treats each entry as a distinct data element. A list cell can hold a mix of text, numbers, dates, and Boolean values while preserving the native data type of each item. An array stores a grid of rows and columns inside one cell. A nested array allows formulas to generate and return arrays inside other arrays. This allows complex outputs to be confined within individual cells instead of trying to spill them across adjacent worksheet rows and columns. These in-cell data structures can simplify complex formula processing and reduce clutter on the worksheet. Availability: These in-cell data structures are available in Excel for Windows and Mac to members of the Microsoft 365 Insider program who are on the Beta Channel. Microsoft has not yet said when the features will begin rolling out to all M365 subscribers, and they are not supported in perpetual license versions (such as Office 2021 or Office 2024) or Excel for the web. Use cases Here are examples of how these three in-cell structures can be used. Multi-item categorizing Imagine categorizing your co-workers, who each have expertise in using up to five M365 software tools: Excel, OneNote, Outlook, PowerPoint, and Word. Or they specialize in selling any number of categories of products. To store this information on a spreadsheet, you could designate a column for each software tool or product category. This of course can take up a lot of columns on the spreadsheet, especially if you have additional columns containing more information about each person. Instead, with an in-cell list, you can store all this information in one column. Excel will recognize each list item individually. These in-cell lists eliminate the need for multiple columns. Howard Wen / Foundry This allows you to filter for one or a combination of these items by clicking the drop-down arrow at the top of the column containing the in-cell list. Because Excel recognizes each item in an in-cell list individually, you can filter the results by the individual items. Howard Wen / Foundry Survey responses contained Say your co-workers or customers are filling out a survey where they rate questions on a numerical scale. Instead of allocating separate columns for each survey question per person, you can store all responses within a single designated cell per respondent. This helps keep the rest of the spreadsheet look cleaner, especially if you’ve designed it with other columns to store additional data about each person. Mitigating #SPILL! errors When using array-processing functions like TEXTSPLIT across an entire column, standard dynamic arrays attempt to spill output values sideways across multiple columns for every row simultaneously. If any blocking data exists in adjacent cells, Excel triggers a #SPILL! error. The array in cell G1 is trying to spill into cell G2, which already has a value. Howard Wen / Foundry Instead, Excel can pack the split outputs inside each respective row’s cell as a nested array. This produces a single-column result that holds all detailed split values internally without spilling across adjacent grid cells or causing formula collisions. The array is now contained in a single cell, eliminating the spill error. articles.title: Windows pushed AI PCs, but now it's hit a wall of RAM prices
articles.content: Microsoft wants enterprise customers to start thinking about PC refreshes using the same mindset – and line in the budget – as AI investments. The problem? Rising component costs caused by the proliferation of AI datacenters mean many clients are delaying client refreshes. In a call to arms, Microsoft became the headline sponsor of the Canalys Forum in Barcelona early last month for the first time ever. Redmond needs distributors and resellers that convene at the event annually to get behind Copilot, Cowork and, more generally, AI computers. Mark Linton, corporate veep for Windows and Device Sales, took to the stage to preach to a room he is hoping to convert. "What we're seeing is the tokenomics of [AI] is getting very challenging," he said. "Having agents working on frontier models quickly becomes very expensive." Redmond's proposed solution is to use those massive LLMs where most needed, "the right model for the right job," running smaller models locally at the edge on Windows PCs. " My goal, if we're successful in pivoting Windows to the agentic platform, is to have PC spend be part of the AI spend versus just PC refresh budget," he said. "In an AI hybrid world, you'll be able to use edge devices, powerful PCs with lots of memory, lots of capability to run your AI workloads that are appropriate right there on the device. You keep the data locally. Of course, you don't have the token cost of the cloud. You have better latency, and you have more control." Copilot is merely a component. This is not only about customers using Microsoft "first-party software" – it's for all models and all agents to use Windows as the platform, added Linton. Goodness knows, Windows does need a shot in the arm. Microsoft last week reported profit and loss accounts for Q1 of its fiscal 2027 , ended September 30, and revenue in the Windows OEM and Devices division shrank 22 percent from last year to $3.55 billion. Microsoft warned revenue generated in its Q2 may be down 30 percent. " Growth will continue to be impacted by elevated inventory levels, PC market demand and a prior year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support," Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on an earnings call. Market watcher IDC said calendar Q3 PC shipments sank to 62.7 million units , down 20.1 percent year-on-year, translating into 15.8 million fewer sales into distributors' warehouses. Tough macroeconomic conditions coupled with rising memory costs mean tough times for the PC industry. Omdia – which owns Canalys – said: " The impact of upstream component cost increases has now fully worked its way through to end-market pricing, with consumers and IT decision-makers responding accordingly." Reg readers know why component costs are going up. The datacenter construction frenzy meant memory chip makers could make more money from higher-margin HBM than conventional DRAM, prompting them to prioritize production of the former . But AI PCs have been a tough sell from the start , as higher prices and a lack of killer applications meant many customers delayed purchases. Microsoft has to convince the market of the benefits – including trade customers as well as those in charge of procurement at enterprises. Once more, the pitch for AI PCs Back at the Canalys Forum, Microsoft's Linton claimed customers mulling AI PC purchases want better productivity, to reduce costs, to innovate, and to be able to use these computers securely and at scale. Microsoft is going to invest heavily in Windows from both the platform capability and security to enable these ends. So, if you are a Microsoft partner, you'll be able to run Windows and secure agents at the operating system level with Agent 365, with Intune, or with Entra. Linton added: " We announced in June some of the technology in Windows, in particular Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC). And so essentially you can virtualize agents, and then you can use Intune to give them policy. And so other platforms, you have to manage agent by…

articles.title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
articles.content: If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn not to enter confidential information . https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988 “[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“ https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review “A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers” https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data “Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.” https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage “Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.” To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours. I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough. Thank you to this user on HN for mentioning in another thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50355424 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50363461 Points: 159 # Comments: 43

articles.title: Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027
articles.content: Starting in 2027, Google plans to turn off AI features in its school products by default, letting schools decide what to enable. The catch: schools that block AI entirely on their devices will also lose access to Google Search, since the two systems are now too deeply intertwined to separate. Given Google's grip on the US school market, that "choice" doesn't leave schools with much room to maneuver. articles.title: Your GitHub Actions Cron Job Can Disappear Without Failing
articles.content: Every morning, a bot posts a short report to Slack: what moved volume and revenue yesterday, driver by driver. It runs on a GitHub Actions schedule and checks its own numbers before it posts. For a small team, it's a good setup. There's no server to babysit, the logs and secrets live in one place, and anyone on the team can read the run history. It's also a scheduler with fine print, and nearly all of the fine print is about the morning the report doesn't arrive. Here's what GitHub's documentation says about scheduled workflows, what it means for a daily report, and the safeguards that make up for it. The fine print These are all in GitHub's docs for the schedule event, roughly in order of how likely they are to bite. Scheduled runs can be late, and some never happen. GitHub warns that scheduled runs can be delayed when Actions is under heavy load, that the start of every hour is one of those times, and that under enough load "some queued jobs may be dropped." A dropped run doesn't fail. It just doesn't happen. Schedules run in UTC unless you say otherwise. Schedules now accept a timezone with an IANA name like America/New_York . Without it, a 7 AM report drifts to 6 AM or 8 AM local twice a year when daylight saving time changes. With it, a time that doesn't exist on the spring-forward day moves to the next valid time. Schedules only run from the default branch , on its latest commit. Editing a workflow on a feature branch won't tell you whether its schedule works. In public repositories, schedules switch off after 60 days with no repository activity. A report that just works for two months and then stops is the most frustrating version of all of this. The shortest interval is five minutes. Irrelevant for a daily report, worth knowing before you build a poller on it. The workflow name: daily-report on: schedule: - cron: "17 7 * * *" # 7:17, not 7:00. The top of the hour is the busiest time. timezone: "America/New_York" # without this, cron runs in UTC workflow_dispatch: # run it by hand when the schedule doesn't concurrency: group: daily-report # a manual run and a scheduled run never overlap cancel-in-progress: false permissions: contents: read jobs: report: runs-on: ubuntu-latest timeout-minutes: 15 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - uses: actions/setup-python@v7 with: python-version: "3.12" - run: pip install -r requirements.txt - run: python -m unittest -q # the QA rules have tests too - run: python main.py env: SLACK_BOT_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SLACK_BOT_TOKEN }} WAREHOUSE_DSN: ${{ secrets.WAREHOUSE_DSN }} Most of those lines answer the fine print. The cron is 17 7 , not 0 7 , because the top of the hour is the busiest time, and a report at 7:17 that arrives beats one at 7:00 that doesn't. workflow_dispatch adds a "Run workflow" button for the mornings the schedule doesn't fire. concurrency stops a manual run and a late scheduled run from overlapping. And the QA rules run as tests before the report does, so a change to the rules can't quietly switch them off. The report checks itself before it posts A daily report should never post a number it can't defend. Before anything goes to the channel, run checks like these: @dataclass class Report: latest_day: date # newest day present in the source data start: float # total for the day before yesterday end: float # yesterday's total drivers: dict = field(default_factory=dict) # what moved it, by driver rows: int = 0 trailing_rows: float = 0 # average daily row count, last 28 days def qa(report, today): problems = [] if report.latest_day < today - timedelta(days=1): problems.append(f"data is stale: newest day is {report.latest_day}") gap = report.start + sum(report.drivers.values()) - report.end if abs(gap) > 1: problems.append(f"drivers don't add up: off by {gap:,.0f}") change = abs(report.end - report.start) or 1 other = abs(report.drivers.get("other", 0)) / change if other > 0.25: problems.append(f"'other' explains {other:.0%} of the change") if report.rows < 0.5 *…

articles.title: Dinosaur Blood Found In Fossils For the First Time
articles.content: Researchers have confirmed the presence of intact biomolecules and mineralized red blood cells inside the 115-million-year-old fossilized bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali from Brazil. The discovery challenges assumptions about how long blood-related biomolecules can survive and could help scientists study dinosaur metabolism, blood evolution and even how traces of ancient life might be preserved on other worlds. Popular Science reports: The evidence exists inside the fossilized limb bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali. Discovered in 2008, A. museunacionali was an Early Cretaceous theropod that lived in present-day northeastern Brazil. The fossils suggest a dinosaur measuring over 10 feet long and weighing about 75 pounds, but given its young age, A. museunacionali likely grew even larger. After carefully examining thin slices of the fossils, paleontologists located the mineralized red blood cell molecular components, along with a complex manganese oxide called hausmannite. This material helped maintain the cellular structures of heme, a ring-shaped molecule that contains iron and binds many proteins, especially hemoglobin. The hausmannite also helped preserve additional biomolecules found in the blood, such as the amino acids in collagen. The study's authors theorize this level of preservation could only occur following a rapid burial in an environment that was rich in microbes, but low in oxygen at the same time. The findings have been published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Datacenter operators must win hearts and minds, not just permits
articles.content: Schneider Electric sees no slowdown in its datacenter business, but says operators must be more open with communities about the power, water, and land their projects will consume. As a supplier of electrical infrastructure, cooling, and power distribution equipment, Schneider has a direct view of operators' spending plans – and a commercial interest in continued construction. Steven Carlini, vice president of innovation and datacenter, said Schneider's pipeline showed no slowdown. "And Schneider has a lot of agreements, supply chain agreements with the larger datacenter operators." Reports earlier this year suggested only half the capacity planned for 2026 is actually under construction in the US, and land being cleared for new bit barn projects has plateaued. Carlini nevertheless said US companies were building as fast as they could, contrasting that with planning bureaucracy and other obstacles in Europe. "But the one thing that I think is going to be the biggest change is the level of transparency from the operators when they're trying to secure permits and when they're requesting power," Carlini said. "The way the model traditionally worked in the US is the operators would negotiate with the local jurisdictions that were responsible for issuing the permits, and there would be non-disclosures involved, almost universally. So the residents where these datacenters were going to be built had no visibility into these projects until construction started." Opposition to datacenter construction has grown in the US. Campaign groups called for a moratorium on new facilities late last year, and New York state imposed a halt this summer. The sheer scale of the new builds has also alarmed many folk, with Meta's Hyperion facility, for example, planned to reach 5 GW of power capacity and cover an area equal to a significant chunk of Manhattan . A recent survey by think tank Pew Research Center found that Americans are increasingly wary of datacenters , with more than half saying they are bad for the environment, bad for household energy bills, and consume water resources for cooling. In response, companies building and operating compute sheds need to be more upfront about what effect their plans will have on the local area, Carlini said. "They're going to have to disclose where the power is going to come from, how they're going to get the power, their water usage, their carbon emissions, the efficiency of the datacenter, where it is going to be located physically, the noise levels of the facility, the water sources, which is a big one, and how much water they're going to use is another big one that operators have traditionally not been very forthright in publishing." In Virginia – the world's "datacenter capital" – an ex-water sustainability program manager at AWS is taking his former employer to court over claims it published false and misleading statements about water use in the state. Carlini expects permitting requirements to force greater disclosure, followed by reporting obligations once facilities are operating. "And then they're going to have to report it as part of regulations during operations as well, so it's not going to be a case of here's our prediction, and then you get the permit and you never have to report again," he said. Datacenter owners and operators must win hearts and minds as well, Carlini added, a point already recognized by some in the industry at an event last year. "From a public relations perspective, that's another area where the operators really need to focus, because in many cases they've taken the position that they're benefiting the community," he said. "Those days are gone, so the operators are going to have to, from a PR perspective, engage with the local residents more amicably." People using Facebook or Gmail doesn't mean they'll welcome a datacenter next door, Carlini told us. "So it's going to have to be more like 'Here's how we're going to help,'" he said. articles.title: A One-Line JavaScript Bug Broke My GA4 Tracking for Five Months
articles.content: For five months, Google Analytics told me nobody on my site ever signed up, converted a file, or bought anything. Page views looked fine. Sessions looked fine. The key events report said zero, every day, and I read that as "the funnel is bad" instead of "the funnel is not being recorded". The bug was one line. This is what it was, why nothing warned me, and how to check your own site in about a minute. The setup I run BatchSet, a set of browser-based image tools. GA4 is loaded the standard way, with the snippet Google gives you: <script async src="https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js?id=G-XXXX"></script> <script> window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || []; function gtag(){dataLayer.push(arguments);} gtag('js', new Date()); gtag('config', 'G-XXXX'); </script> Custom events came from a small typed helper in the app code, so components could call trackEvent({ action: "sign_up" }) instead of touching window directly: function gtag(...args: unknown[]) { if (typeof window === "undefined") return const w = window as unknown as { dataLayer?: unknown[] } w.dataLayer = w.dataLayer || [] w.dataLayer.push(args) } export function trackEvent({ action, params }: GTagEvent) { gtag("event", action, params) } It looks like a faithful TypeScript port of the snippet. It is not. The difference Google's gtag() pushes arguments . Mine pushed args . arguments is an array-like object. Its type is [object Arguments] . ...args is a rest parameter, and that gives you a real Array . They hold the same values in the same order, and in DevTools they look almost identical: Object.prototype.toString.call(arguments) // "[object Arguments]" Object.prototype.toString.call(args) // "[object Array]" gtag.js does not treat those two the same. I tested it on the live site: pushing an array sent no hit at all, and pushing an Arguments object with the same three values sent the event. No console error, no warning, no failed request. The array just sat in dataLayer and was never acted on. I can't point you to a line in Google's docs that says "arrays are ignored". I can tell you what happened on a real production site, and that the fix changed the result. Why nothing warned me Three things hid it. Page views kept working. The config call comes from Google's own snippet, which uses arguments . So page_view , session_start , first_visit , scroll and user_engagement all arrived. The dashboard looked alive. Only the events from my own helper were missing. dataLayer looked full. If you open the console and type dataLayer , you see your events sitting there with the right names and parameters. That feels like proof. It only proves the push happened, not that anything read it. Modern style pushes you toward the bug. Rest parameters are the idiomatic way to write variadic functions now. ESLint even has a core rule, prefer-rest-params , that flags use of arguments . Writing the "clean" version is exactly what breaks it. On top of that, zero is a believable number for a small site. I had a funnel I had designed and instrumented, and when it read zero I started theorising about why people were leaving, not about whether the instrument worked. That cost more time than the bug itself. The fix function gtag(..._args: unknown[]) { if (typeof window === "undefined") return const w = window as unknown as { dataLayer?: unknown[] } w.dataLayer = w.dataLayer || [] // Must be the Arguments object, like Google's snippet. // gtag.js does not act on plain arrays. w.dataLayer.push(arguments) } The ..._args parameter is only there so TypeScript accepts calls with arguments. The value that gets pushed is arguments . If you use prefer-rest-params , turn it off for that line and leave a comment, or the next tidy-up will put the bug back. The simpler option is to not write your own wrapper at all and call window.gtag(...) , which is Google's function. I kept the wrapper because it also does a server-side usage record and a consent check, but if yours does nothing extra, delete it. I also added…

articles.title: What happens to your online accounts when you die? Here’s how to prepare
articles.content: What happens to all of your online accounts—credit cards, merchants, news subscriptions, social media, streaming services—after you die? How will your heirs know how to access these accounts or understand what you want done with them? Most people haven’t considered these questions, and this lack of planning can create significant headaches for next of kin. We studied challenges older adults encounter when thinking about what should happen to their online accounts after they die. We interviewed 21 American adults over age 60 to learn about their concerns, needs, and practices for their online accounts, as well as what would make planning for these accounts easier. Most of the people we interviewed had hired lawyers or estate planners to draft wills specifying how their money and physical property should be handled after their deaths. They wanted to make sure that heirs had easy access to the money and assets left behind. People also wanted their relatives to have easy access to their digital estates, but they had not done any formal planning and didn’t know how to plan for transitioning or shutting down online accounts, such as email, social media, and accounts for online bills. Some told us they hadn’t thought about their online accounts at all. Others said they assumed heirs would know what to do, or they assumed that giving heirs the passwords to accounts would be enough to grant access to their digital estates. Unfortunately, more planning is typically necessary to smoothly transition a digital estate. Passing down a list of passwords The older adults we interviewed mainly kept track of their passwords by hand: They wrote their passwords down on paper, or they stored them in a digital file. Almost everyone had already shared some of their passwords with family members who help them manage their accounts. Everyone also believed that their heirs would be able to find their list of passwords after their death. The people we interviewed weren’t always happy with their current systems for keeping track of their passwords. Some people complained that when accounts required frequent password changes, it was difficult to keep their password lists up to date . As a result, they weren’t sure their heirs would get the latest version of all their passwords. Password managers can be a good way to make sure passwords are up to date and, if set up appropriately, accessible to a designated heir. While most of the people we interviewed used password managers, some said they didn’t save important passwords in them because they didn’t know whether they were secure . However, using a password manager is the most frequent security recommendation from experts , who typically use them to store passwords for all of their accounts. By using a password manager, you can make sure your designated heir has access to all your latest passwords. Some password managers provide access for survivors by default, such as through time-delayed emergency access features . You can also write the master password down somewhere safe to pass to your heir. Instead of making sure dozens of account passwords are up to date, you only have to manage one. Passwords alone cannot unlock all accounts Unfortunately, just handing someone your passwords doesn’t always mean they can log in and manage your account. If the account asks for two-factor authentication, such as through a code sent to a phone or email, a password alone won’t grant access. And if the email account is closed or the phone number is no longer active after you die, then they might be out of luck . To make sure your heirs aren’t locked out, identify the devices and accounts that can act as keys for heirs to unlock the rest of your online accounts, and direct your heirs to keep them open until other accounts have been settled. This not only makes sure that heirs can get authentication codes, but also lets heirs reset passwords to your other accounts if they can’t find the password. In some cases, passwords…

articles.title: Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air: Edge0's 0.6B Multilingual Text-to-Speech Model Explained
articles.content: Overview Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air is Edge0’s 0.6B multilingual text-to-speech model for speech generation with or without a reference voice. It supports zero-shot voice cloning from reference audio and its exact transcript, and lists 23 supported languages. Maintained by Edge0. Best use cases Generate speech from text in the 23 listed languages, or clone a voice using a clean reference recording and matching transcript. It can also be deployed through an SGLang Omni adapter with an OpenAI-compatible speech API. Limitations Language quality varies. Reported error-rate and speaker-similarity metrics assess intelligibility and similarity, not perceived realism; the supplied evaluation does not directly quantify realism. Runtime checks were performed on an NVIDIA H20 in BF16, but throughput and streaming were not benchmarked. The model uses custom Transformers code, so loading requires trust_remote_code=True ; review repository files before enabling it. How it compares Compared with the earlier Preview release, Realistic Air adds 12 supported languages (23 versus 11). On the reported Seed-TTS aggregate, its error rate is 1.25% versus Preview’s 1.23%, while SIM is 0.704 versus 0.682; the releases were evaluated separately. On the shared eight-language CV3 subset, Realistic Air reports 4.56% error versus Preview’s 4.80%. The supplied reference comparison cautions that different evaluation pipelines and text normalization prevent a strictly matched ranking. Other Audio8 versions include Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b, Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b, and Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.1b; the supplied evidence does not establish detailed capability differences for those alternatives. Technical specifications DualAR architecture: a slow autoregressive transformer predicts one semantic token per audio frame; a fast autoregressive transformer predicts codec codebooks conditioned on the slow hidden state and preceding codebooks. Main model: 601,159,424 parameters, excluding the separately bundled codec. Slow AR: 24 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads. Fast AR: 4 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads. Audio uses 10 codebooks with 4,096 entries each. The codec operates at 44.1 kHz and 2,048 samples per model frame (about 21.5 frames/s); context is up to 2,048 packed text/audio positions. The repository includes the checkpoint, codec, tokenizer, processor, and custom Transformers code. Python 3.10 or newer and a CUDA-capable GPU are recommended. Runtime smoke tests used PyTorch 2.8.0, Transformers 4.57.3, and an NVIDIA H20 with BF16. License metadata specifies Apache-2.0. Model inputs and outputs Inputs Text is passed to the processor as a list. For voice cloning, provide reference audio and a transcript that exactly matches the spoken content; a clean recording is recommended. Reference-free generation needs only text. The example uses max_new_tokens , temperature , top_p , top_k , and do_sample as generation controls. Supported languages: Cantonese, Chinese, Dutch, English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Spanish, Arabic, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Malay, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Thai, Turkish, and Vietnamese. Outputs Generation returns audio codes that are decoded by the bundled codec into waveforms. The example writes a WAV file at model.config.codec_sample_rate . The SGLang Omni adapter supports a non-streaming OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech API, reference-free generation, and zero-shot voice cloning. articles.title: How I Built an AI-Powered Hacker News Book Recommendation Site in 2.5 Hours
articles.content: On 1 Nov, Andrej Karpathy shared HackerTube (https://hackertube.org/). He had Claude filter 43M Hacker News comments from 20 years down to 6,454 recommended videos, and he said the site took about 2 hours with Opus 5.5 in Claude Code. He also published the data as a public zip. As a Lead SWE, my first question was whether I could pull off the same trick with a different topic and a different tool. I picked books, because HN comment threads are basically one long reading list. I picked Cursor, because that's the tool I use every day. The result is HackerShelf: https://ishankdev.github.io/hackershelf/ (code: https://github.com/IshankDev/hackershelf). How Karpathy's pipeline works His DATA.md lays out the method, and I copied it: Scan every HN comment from 2007 to 2026 in the open-index/hacker-news dataset for YouTube links. The comment needs at least 100 characters of its own text. Keep a video only if at least 3 different people mentioned it in at least 3 different months. Claude Sonnet 5.5 labels each mention with a stance, topics, a reason and a quote. Sonnet writes a card for each video, then puts it into 1 to 3 categories. Opus 5.5 in Claude Code runs the whole thing. He did a few steps by hand: a Google Cloud API key for YouTube metadata, a VPS and a domain. My version: HackerShelf Same idea, but for books: Source: HN comments from Jan 2024 to Aug 2026 from open-index/hacker-news, 9,437,609 comments in total Pre-filter: DuckDB regex for book links (Amazon, Goodreads, Open Library, Bookshop, ISBNs, O'Reilly, Manning, PragProg, No Starch) and phrases like "must read", "worth a read" and "book called". This took about 9 seconds and left 11,519 candidates. Extraction: gemini-3.5-flash-lite in 288 batches of 40 found 6,076 book mentions. Resolve: Open Library matched 2,212 works. Using Karpathy's rule (at least 3 people, at least 3 months), 151 books were left. Cards: one Gemini call per book, so 151 calls Site: a static site on GitHub Pages The final shelf has 151 books, 723 mentions and 601 unique recommenders , sorted into 9 categories. Time: Karpathy's 2 hours vs. mine Being honest, my total was longer than his. Planning and data checks: 7:47 to 7:50 PM IST Cursor build (pipeline code, the full site and deploy setup): about 40 minutes, 7:56 to 8:37 PM IST Gemini extraction: about 20 minutes, about 8:50 to 9:11 PM IST Open Library resolve and filter: about 44 minutes, 9:24 to 10:08 PM IST, with no LLM. This was the slowest step. Cards: 509 seconds, 10:09 to 10:17 PM IST Site data: under 1 second, at 10:17 PM IST From start to finish that's about 2.5 hours of wall clock (7:47 to about 10:17 PM IST). That includes my own manual steps: creating the repo, giving Cursor GitHub access and turning on GitHub Pages. Cursor's part, writing the actual code, took about 40 minutes. Most of the remaining time went to calling APIs and waiting on rate limits. Cost Tokens: 1,968,177 in and 623,943 out What I paid: $0, on Gemini's free tier. I hit 429s and handled them with backoff and retry. Paid-rate equivalent: at $0.30 in and $2.50 out per 1M tokens, about $0.59 + $1.56 = about $2.15 Cursor usage cost: I don't know this number yet, so I won't guess. What went wrong The first Cursor run shipped sample data. The site worked, but it only had 9 placeholder books. The real data had to come from a separate run of the LLM stage. Too many candidates. The first broad filter matched about 392k comments that might mention a book, which was far too many for a free tier. Tighter link and phrase rules cut that down to 11,519. The model paraphrased. 470 of the extracted "quotes" weren't actually word for word in the source comment. I didn't trust them, so I blanked them. Open Library isn't perfect. One top-10 entry resolved as "1984 (adaptation)" by Michael Dean instead of Orwell's novel. Fuzzy title matching is the weak link here. Does it hold up? I spot-checked 10 books and 83 mentions against the original HN comments. 83 out of 83 had the right…

articles.title: Agent Graph Engineering, Part 5: How to Build Safer AI Agents With Structured Errors and Guardrails
articles.content: TL;DR Two edges, one idea: constrain the model declaratively rather than by inspecting what it produced. A tool is a function plus metadata, and it signals failure by raising a structured error, never by returning a string the model has to interpret. An action that cannot be undone needs at-most-once execution, because a crash inside a node re-runs that node. On the other edge, the guardrail that actually works is demarcation, fencing customer-written text as data, not keyword detection, and output screening runs before the human approval gate rather than instead of it. Part 4 covered the agent and the flow that routes it. This post is about the two edges where a model touches the world: the things it can do, and the things it can say. They belong together because the mistake is the same on both sides, which is trying to fix bad behavior by reading the output rather than by shaping what is possible. Part one: what it may do The error string problem Here is the version almost everyone writes first: async def issue_refund(charge_id: str) -> str: try: except Exception as e: return f"Error: could not issue refund ({e})" Returning the error feels right, because the model needs to know it failed. It does. The problem is what else now depends on that sentence. The model reads it and decides what to do next, so your retry logic is now a model inferring intent from English. Your frontend wants to show a different card for “rate limited” than for “card declined”, so somebody writes if "rate limit" in result.lower() . Then you reword the message for clarity and three things break silently, none of which have tests, because the tests also match on the prose. Worse, a genuine bug becomes indistinguishable from a handled failure. A ZeroDivisionError in your refund maths comes back as "Error: could not issue refund" , the model apologizes politely to the customer, and nothing pages anyone. Raise, never return So tools raise, and a decorator converts: class ToolError(Exception): """Base for structured tool failures. `message` is LLM-facing and may carry technical detail. `user_message` is what a human sees; it defaults to the message when not given. """ error_type = "tool_error" def __init__(self message: str *user_message: str | None = None) -> None: super().__init__(message) selfmessage = message selfuser_message = user_message or message class InvalidInputError(ToolError): error_type = "invalid_input" class RateLimitedError(ToolError): error_type = "rate_limited" class UpstreamServiceError(ToolError): """A dependency failed: 5xx, timeout, DNS, connection reset.""" error_type = "upstream_service_error" The wrapper catches ToolError and turns it into a result carrying a machine-readable error_type . Callers branch on the type. Nobody parses a sentence. Two properties fall out, and the second one took me an incident to appreciate. Two audiences, one failure. message is what the model sees and can be as technical as you like. user_message is what a person sees, and it falls back to message when a tool does not bother. Collapsing them into one string means either leaking internals to a customer or starving the model of what it needs to recover. The refund ceiling is the clearest case: raise InvalidInputError( f"issue_refund called with amount={amount}, over the " f"£{MAX_SELF_SERVE:.0f} self-serve ceiling." user_message=( f"Refunds over £{MAX_SELF_SERVE:.0f} have to go through finance." ) ) The model is told the argument it passed and the limit it broke, which is what it needs to decide whether to retry with a smaller amount or escalate. The customer is told the policy. Neither sentence would do both jobs. Anything that is not a ToolError propagates. That is deliberate and it is the important half. A ZeroDivisionError is a bug, not a handled failure, and converting it into a tidy tool result is how you ship a system that silently does the wrong thing and looks healthy. Let it crash, let the run fail loudly, and find out. Metadata is what makes…

articles.title: The Prompt Engineering Trick That Could Be Making Your AI Slower
articles.content: Introduction A common meme in the LLM community is to instruct a model to “make no mistakes”, implying that telling a model to act a certain way can greatly improve the final result. In this vein, an oft-cited rule in prompt engineering is to give the model a role to play 1 . For example: “You are an expert in physics. Now answer this physics question.” This is called “persona” prompting. While persona prompting can work for output style — e.g. prompting an LLM to act like a caveman 2 can reduce the length and complexity of its responses — it’s often assumed that personas can also improve the factual accuracy of a model’s answer. A couple months ago, I tested the persona prompting theory in a small experiment I posted about on LinkedIn . When this suggested little to no improvement, I decided to expand the test. Before we dive into the full experiment though, it’s important to understand the current gaps in existing persona prompting research. Existing Research The effect of personas on factual accuracy has been studied in academic literature. In “Prompting Science Report 4: Playing Pretend” 3 , researchers tested six language models on two multiple-choice scientific question benchmarks. They found that applying expert personas had little to no effect on the accuracy of the answers, while low knowledge personas — such as “act like a toddler” — reduced accuracy. In “Scientific Agents:…” 4 , Timothy Kassis from K-Dense evaluated a repository of 503 profession-specific AGENTS.md profiles using Gemini 3.8 flash. Across nine separate text-based benchmarks, Kassis found the average accuracy saw no statistically clear improvement from the baseline, but models used 1.5 to 2.3 times as many output tokens. “When ‘A Helpful Assistant’ Is Not Really Helpful” 5 found similar results, with 162 personas across 2410 questions demonstrating no reliable improvement in performance. “Expert Personas Improve LLM Alignment but Damage Accuracy” 6 found that personas can be useful for improving safety alignment to increase refusal rates, but that they otherwise had a neutral or even damaging effect on factual accuracy, depending on the model and the placement of the prompt. “Principled Personas” 7 explored personas across different model sizes, finding no improvement from expert personas except in highly specific cases, and irrelevant personas had a significant negative effect. The existing literature points toward prompting with an expert persona having little to no positive effect and in some cases a negative effect. However, previous work appears to focus mainly on factual accuracy, leaving cost and speed as afterthoughts. Practical Implications In the real world where LLMs are being used to solve real-world problems, engineers are recommended to include persona-like prompts in production systems 1 , 8 . Even worse, personas are often baked into system prompts or included in harness defaults, so the end user might not even know they’re there at all 9 . The choices for practitioners, then, are whether to adopt persona prompting in bespoke systems and whether it’s worth the effort to remove personas from existing software retroactively. The studies tell us that, solely for factual accuracy, personas don’t have an effect either way. But with the increasing relevance of cost and speed in production LLM applications, it’s important to ask: how does persona prompting affect cost and speed? Does adding a persona increase the cost you pay per answer or the time it takes to get an answer back? The Experiment To answer this question, I designed an experiment to measure accuracy, cost, and speed across four models and five personas. I randomly sampled a set of 5000 multiple-choice questions across nine subject areas from the MMLU-Pro dataset 10 and ran the models with each persona across the question set. Each model completion request included one of five conditions in the system prompt field: Neutral: “You are a helpful assistant. You are always glad to…

articles.title: AI-search Results Are Emerging As An Important Influencer and Creator Discovery Tool
articles.content: Until recently, creators and influencers could boost their visibility and their potential earnings by winning the search battleground on Instagram, TikTok, or Google. But a shift in search behavior is reshaping creator and influencer discovery. AI-powered search has emerged and is drawing more and more people away from traditional search tools, which means the pathways people use to find creators are shifting. And the shift affects more than just efforts to add more followers. Those in the creator marketplace now must contend with the fact that agencies are increasingly using AI tools to identify creators, while marketers are beginning to build AI visibility into creator briefs and partnership strategies. Adjusting to this shift is important, but experts say the evolution of search behavior won't impact all creators equally. “How AI search affects creators depends a lot on the type of content and the platform they’re on,” says Max Anderson , Owner and CEO of OnlyFinder , the leading search engine for OnlyFans launched in 2020. Anderson’s work is focused on creator discovery, ad-tech, digital marketplace economics, consumer behavior, and the data behind how users find and engage with creators online. Through OnlyFinder, a search and discovery platform built around the creator economy, he brings a data-driven perspective on OnlyFans trends, search behavior, monetization, and digital publishing. “For informational queries, for example, AI is simply a better experience,” Anderson says. “Instead of clicking through 10 blue links and scanning pages for an answer, you ask and get it, and that cannibalizes a very large share of informational search. So if your business is influencer marketing involving informational content, it’s at risk because LLMs will answer those questions directly, and they may or may not cite you. But information retrieval is only one mode of internet behavior.” How creators and influencers can avoid being sidelined by AI search Adjusting to how AI search is changing the way people find creators starts with understanding where AI search shines and where it struggles. As Anderson mentions above, AI search is a huge help to those who are looking for information. But analytics derived from recent research show that informational searches account for just over half of the searches people make on Google. And AI search isn’t the best for the other half. “People go online to shop, comparing options, photos and data side by side, which carries far more commercial value,” Anderson points out. “And they go online to be entertained, to sit back and browse. AI is a much worse experience for both of those.” The limitations Anderson mentions above suggest creators can avoid being sidelined by being intentional about the way they package their content. Getting direct views, rather than being filtered through AI search results, requires offering experiences that AI isn’t adept at providing. “The pivot for creators is to offer experiences that don’t make sense inside an LLM interface,” Anderson says. “For example, if you’re providing long-form video that a person actually wants to watch, people will opt for that over an AI-generated synopsis of your video.” Anderson also points out that the category of content can have an impact on the degree to which creators are affected by AI search. For example, while everyday tasks and academic subjects are core categories for AI search, queries about NSFW topics are often declined. “If you’re among the nearly 5 million OnlyFans creators, for example, you’re largely unaffected by AI search because, as a matter of policy, the major AI tools won’t answer those questions,” Anderson says. “Ask Google, or a vertical search engine like OnlyFinder, for the best redhead OnlyFans creators, and you get a ranked list of exactly what you wanted. Ask ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, and they decline.” How to connect with companies that use AI search as a creator discovery tool While AI’s effect on finding…

articles.title: Understanding Software PLCs: Architecture, Execution, and Security Boundaries
articles.content: Why I Started with the Foundations When I finished my industrial protocol research series, I wanted to move closer to the systems using those protocols. I turned my attention to software PLCs and started investigating OpenPLC Runtime v4. My first investigation quickly took me into runtime internals and the Linux environment supporting them. There was a lot to learn, but I eventually realised that I was spending more time understanding implementation details than answering the security questions I had originally set out to explore. I stepped back and reorganised the project. Before investigating how software PLCs could be attacked, I wanted to understand what they actually are, how they operate, and how their different components fit together. That became Part I: Software PLC Foundations. Understanding the Software PLC A Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) is an industrial computing system responsible for monitoring inputs, executing control logic, and controlling outputs connected to a physical process. It receives information from devices such as sensors, evaluates that information against its programmed instructions, and sends commands to equipment such as motors, pumps, and valves. Traditionally, PLC functionality has been delivered through dedicated industrial controller hardware. A typical controller brings together a CPU, memory, system software, communication interfaces, and connections to industrial I/O. Depending on the platform, these components may be integrated into a compact unit or arranged as a modular system. A Software PLC (SoftPLC) implements the same fundamental control functionality through a software runtime operating on a compatible computing platform. That platform might be an industrial PC, an embedded computer, or another supported computing environment. This contrast became the starting point for my first investigation. A software PLC still relies on physical hardware. What changes is how the controller functionality is implemented and how it relates to the underlying computing environment. In a traditional PLC, the manufacturer generally delivers the controller as an integrated platform with its own firmware, execution environment, and supported hardware interfaces. In a SoftPLC, the runtime depends more directly on the host platform. The operating environment supplies computing resources and system services, while the runtime provides the environment for loading and executing the control application. That separation introduces some interesting possibilities. Software PLCs can offer more flexibility in hardware selection and integration with other software systems. It also means that the host operating environment becomes part of the controller's architecture and something we need to understand when examining its security. The deployment model adds another layer to this picture. A software PLC can run directly on a host operating system, use a real-time operating environment, or operate inside a virtual machine or container. These arrangements are quite different. A virtual machine provides a guest operating system over virtualised hardware managed by a hypervisor. A container packages and isolates application processes while sharing the host operating system's kernel. That difference is important. The isolation provided by a container is not the same as the separation between a virtual machine and its host. Access to devices, network interfaces, filesystems, and host resources also depends on how the environment is configured. I also wanted to understand the assumptions around execution timing. There is a tendency to associate deterministic control exclusively with dedicated PLC hardware, as though running control software on a general-purpose platform automatically makes predictable execution impossible. The reality is more dependent on the complete configuration. Processor resources, scheduling, operating system behaviour, runtime implementation, I/O handling, and competing workloads all…

articles.title: Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission
articles.content: An artist’s conception shows Starfish Space’s Otter spacecraft in orbit. (Starfish Space Illustration) Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end. In a LinkedIn post , the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability ( SSPICY ). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said. The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said. However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said. Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable. In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters. “Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.” Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.” “Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.” Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force . Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year . Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”
articles.author: Alan Boyle
articles.fingerprint: contact ending inspection loses mission otter satellite space spacecraft starfish
